audit:note-voice (#1089) asks a neighbouring question of the same field and reports 7, because its cue matches `confirmed via research` but not `Confirmed via Mountain Project`. That gap was flagged to that lane; the DATA half is done here.

Only `note` was changed. Every waypoint is returned in its original order with lat/lng/elev/type/name byte-identical - a lost or moved pin would silently break the map and the base-finding, so the verifier checks structure before it checks prose.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Corrected - previous waypoints incorrectly placed this route ~59 miles away at Amphitheater Mountain (Pasayten Wilderness), a research error. South Peak is actually part of the Gunsight Range, Glacier Peak Wilderness - same remote 2-day approach as Middle Peak (Downey/Bachelor Creek trail to Itswoot Ridge, Dome-Chickamin col, Chickamin Glacier).

waypoints.name: South Peak (Gunsight Range)
waypoints.note: The southernmost of four named summits (Northeast/North/Middle/South) along one short ridge crest, reached last in a north-to-south traverse after Middle Peak. This coordinate is a geometric estimate about 0.2mi south of Middle Peak along the ridge, not a surveyed fix.

waypoints.name: High Bridge / Agnes Creek (Stehekin access)
waypoints.note: Glacier Peak Wilderness, accessed from Stehekin via High Bridge/Agnes Creek. This is the Stehekin-side access point, not a dedicated trailhead.

waypoints.name: Tye Road / Old Stevens Pass Highway pullout (near double hairpin turn, ~1.4 mi from US 2)
waypoints.note: From Hwy 2 at Stevens Pass, take old Stevens Pass Hwy/Tye Rd downhill toward Wellington and pull off just uphill of the double hairpin turn, ~1.4 mi from US2. This coordinate is an estimated pulloff location consistent with those written directions rather than a surveyed pin.
waypoints.directions: Take US-2 east out of Seattle or Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway, now signed Tye Road, which runs toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite. Follow it roughly 1.4 miles from US-2 and park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn. Allow about half an hour of driving.

waypoints.name: Half Moon Crag
waypoints.note: Granite crag visible from Highway 2, ~45-60min/1,000ft approach through old-growth forest. Routes are short (≤85 ft), so this single coordinate serves as both approach reference and topout.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road-end parking; recorded coordinates vary slightly, between 48.9105,-121.5894 and 48.9102,-121.592, but describe the same location.

waypoints.name: Top of Mamie Peak wall
waypoints.note: Blood Orgy is reached by rappel off Woodland Critter Christmas, or via a short 5.10 pitch starting up it; Mamie Peak's true summit (6,108') is easy scrambling above.

waypoints.name: Alpental Ski Area / Snow Lake Trailhead parking lot
waypoints.note: Blood Sport is reached by heading up the boot path/old Sahale ski track from this lot and traversing east along the base of Guye Peak's south rib — the route is passed while traversing east along the base of the South Rib.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 exit 52 and follow Alpental Road to its end at the Alpental ski area lot, which is also the Snow Lake Trailhead parking — about 45 minutes from Seattle. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private-property sections of the road on the way up. From the lot it is only about half a mile of walking, roughly 15 minutes, so this is a park-and-go rather than an approach.

waypoints.name: Blood Sport crag
waypoints.note: Short (~50') isolated crag low on the mountain, just around the corner from the main West Face, near the base of South Rib.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small pullout on Cascade River Road, mile ~21.7, opposite Johannesburg Mountain. The Southeast Face is reached by climbing up from Boston Basin high camp toward the Sahale/Quien Sabe Glacier area and traversing to the face, not via a separate road trailhead.
waypoints.directions: The start is a small pullout on Cascade River Road at about mile 21.7, roughly 3,200 ft, opposite Johannesburg Mountain. There is no separate road trailhead for the Southeast Face — the face is reached from Boston Basin high camp, so this pullout is where you park. Camping in the basin needs an NPS wilderness permit registered through Marblemount, and the sites are popular enough to be worth arranging ahead for July through September.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Gated old Monte Cristo Road starts here; $5/day or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass required at the self-issue kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Barlow Pass is where the pavement ends on the Mountain Loop Highway. The old Monte Cristo road beyond the gate is closed to cars but open to bikes, and most parties ride it to save their legs for the scramble.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo Townsite
waypoints.note: End of the 4-mile gated gravel road (bike or hike); pick up the Glacier Basin/Glacier Creek trail heading east out of the old mining townsite.
waypoints.directions: Four miles of gently rising gravel road following the South Fork Sauk River. There is a bike rack under the trees at the townsite end; leave the bike there and walk through the old town. Bridges and creek crossings on this stretch have washed out before, so expect the odd detour.

waypoints.name: Ray's Knoll, Glacier Basin
waypoints.note: Timbered knoll in the middle of the basin used as the standard camp; treat water carefully as old mine tailings have contaminated basin runoff with heavy metals.
waypoints.directions: Cross the footbridge on the far side of the townsite and follow signs onto the Glacier Basin Trail, which climbs steadily beside Glacier Creek past a prominent waterfall before easing off into the basin. Aim for the prominent hummock in the middle of the basin. Early in the season the last of this holds patchy snow.

waypoints.name: Erosion gully to headwall waterfall
waypoints.note: Ascend the obvious mine-tailings-colored erosion gully on Cadet's SW face to a headwall with a small waterfall; loose rock underfoot, stay climbers' left of the falls.
waypoints.directions: Find a safe place to ford Glacier Creek — it can be a swift, cold wade during snowmelt — then navigate by the two large boulders: an approximately 15-ft one marks the start of the scramble, and a bigger one across the basin is the next mark. From there start up the reddish blown-out gully, climbing the rib that separates it from the deeper gully immediately to its left. Cairns and occasional flagging carry on where the maintained tread ends.

waypoints.name: Cliff-band crux ledge
waypoints.note: Traverse sharply left on a moderately exposed Class 3 ledge to find the correct notch through the cliff band; easy to lose on the way down.
waypoints.directions: About 25 ft below the waterfall headwall, break out of the gully to climber's left onto a band of red rock. It reads as a dead end from below, and it is the one feature parties lose on the way down — worth building a duck or cairn as you pass through it.

waypoints.name: Southwest ridge crest
waypoints.note: Climber's path exits the brush/scrub onto the ridge crest here; follow heather slopes northeast toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the ledges upward through scrub trees and brush, then pick up the faint climbers' path that switchbacks the rest of the way onto the crest.

waypoints.name: Cadet Peak
waypoints.note: True summit register; the subsidiary South Cadet high point is a short detour back along the SW ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest northeast — loose in places, but easy route-finding. Do not be drawn into the deep gully well to climber's left; it is a hazardous false lead. Around 6,500 ft a distinctive hobbit-like rock feature marks a sharp left turn onto a loose talus traverse that runs below the rock and out to the summit ridge. One or two short class 3-4 moves are typical near the top, and everything up here throws rock, so avoid stacking directly below another party.

waypoints.name: Phelps Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trail #1511 starts on an old mining road; self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at Coles Corner take WA-207 north, then Chiwawa River Road (FR-62) about 22 miles — paved for the first eleven, gravel and rough after that — and finish with 2.3 miles up Phelps Creek Road (FR-6211) to the road end. Low-clearance vehicles struggle on the last stretch. Cloudy Pass can also be reached from Holden Village up Railroad Creek or from Trinity over Buck Creek Pass, but both are longer multi-day alternatives; the waypoints below follow the Phelps Creek line.

waypoints.name: Leroy Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Largest of roughly 16 creek crossings on the approach and often the wettest ford; an unmaintained climbers' path branches here toward Leroy Basin.
waypoints.directions: Follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 up the valley on an old mining grade, crossing into the Glacier Peak Wilderness around the two-and-a-half-mile mark. The grade is gentle and Phelps Creek runs alongside the whole way, so water is never a concern. Leroy Creek is the largest of the tributary crossings and the one most likely to soak your feet; the unmaintained path climbing toward Leroy Basin leaves here and is not your turn.

waypoints.name: Spider Meadow
waypoints.note: Broad subalpine meadow with established camps at its upper end; no campfires allowed (prohibited above 4,000 ft).
waypoints.directions: Stay on #1511 as the valley opens out — roughly 1,900 ft of gain over the six and a half miles from the car, so this is easy ground. The meadow is the last flat, sheltered camping before the climb to the gap, and it is the obvious place to stage from if you are not going car-to-car.

waypoints.name: Spider Gap / Spider Glacier remnant
waypoints.note: Unmaintained, cairned route climbs steep loose scree then crosses a permanent snowfield (the shrinking Spider Glacier) to the gap; microspikes and an ice axe are recommended even in summer.
waypoints.directions: Above the meadow the trail climbs into upper Phelps Basin and the maintained tread gives out; a cairned, unmaintained line goes up steep loose scree to the base of the snow around 5,300 ft. From there about half a mile of permanent snowfield leads to the gap. It generally boots or plunge-steps easily in summer, but early season brings open crevasses and firm refrozen snow, and a whiteout or a morning refreeze turns the axe and traction from optional into necessary.

waypoints.name: Cloudy Pass
waypoints.note: Broad meadow saddle above the Lyman Lakes basin where the climbers' trail toward Cloudy Peak's southwest ridge leaves the maintained Cloudy Pass Trail #1256.
waypoints.directions: Descend the north side of the gap. The first hundred vertical feet are the steepest, with the softer, less sun-affected snow usually on the climber's-left (north) side, and it eases into scree and then a gentler snowfield. Follow the basin down past the Lyman Glacier and the Upper Lyman Lakes to Lower Lyman Lake, then climb back up through open meadows to the pass — several miles for a modest net loss and regain, and the pass is the normal camp for the peak.

waypoints.name: Southwest ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Climbers' path through meadows fades into heather benches and then talus; aim for the broad crest of the southwest ridge above the pass.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and head roughly north-northeast up open wildflower meadows on an obvious boot path. The path fades onto heather benches and then talus; keep working toward the broad crest of the southwest ridge rather than contouring across the slopes below it.

waypoints.name: Notch below the summit block
waypoints.note: A notch separates the ridge from the summit block, blocking the direct line; traverse climber's-right around to the north side of the block to find the scramble route (helmet recommended - falls here would be serious).
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest of the ridge itself. Straying onto the flanking slopes drops you into seriously unstable scree that is both slower and harder to reverse, and the crest falls away sharply on its far (north) side. Pick a deliberate line through the loose talus blocks — this is exactly the terrain for knocking rock onto a partner, so spread out and keep helmets on.

waypoints.name: Cloudy Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained by a short, exposed Class 3-4 scramble on the north side of the block; first climbed in 1921 by a Mountaineers party.
waypoints.directions: The notch blocks the direct line, so traverse climber's-right around the east side of the summit block and keep going onto its north (back) side, where a short Class 3-4 weakness leads to the top. It is narrow with real exposure and is the technical crux of the route; cautious parties rope the last few moves.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required at the self-issue kiosk; gated Monte Cristo Road begins here and can be hiked or biked.
waypoints.directions: From the Verlot Public Service Center follow the Mountain Loop Highway east about 19.5 miles to the large parking area at Barlow Pass. The highway is paved the whole way now, and the lot fills on summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo Townsite
waypoints.note: Historic ghost-town ruins; do not drink water here or below the site — arsenic from 1890s mine tailings contaminates the soil and creek.
waypoints.directions: Step around the gate and follow the old Monte Cristo mining road east for roughly four miles. It is a wide, nearly flat roadbed with only about 500 ft of gain, so many parties bike it and save an hour in each direction. Expect a washout reroute near the start and a log/footbridge crossing of the South Fork Sauk about a mile in; the road simply ends at the ruins.

waypoints.name: First safe water past the townsite
waypoints.note: Safe drinking water resumes roughly a mile beyond Monte Cristo, once you're clear of the old tailings.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the signed Poodle Dog Pass / Twin Lakes trail behind the townsite and start climbing switchbacks. Carry whatever water you need out of the valley below rather than filling here — it takes about a mile of gain above the site to get clear of the old tailings.

waypoints.name: Poodle Dog Pass
waypoints.note: Trail junction just above Silver Lake — a 0.4 mi spur drops right to Silver Lake while the Twin Lakes Trail climbs left toward the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Keep grinding the switchbacks, roughly 1,600 ft in about a mile and a half from the townsite, to the signed pass on the ridge.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trail ridge high point
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here (its high point) and head east along the ridge toward Columbia's west spur rather than dropping to Twin Lakes.
waypoints.directions: Ignore the spur dropping right to Silver Lake and take the Twin Lakes Trail left, climbing and contouring along the ridge. It is decently graded but sees less maintenance than the trail below — expect deadfall — and crosses granite slabs higher up. Sunday Creek, about 1.25 miles before Twin Lakes, is the last reliable water on the route; the high point comes before the trail starts losing elevation into the lakes basin.

waypoints.name: SW-face gully below the cliff band
waypoints.note: Wide, loose talus gully with a couple of class 4 moves to enter — notable rockfall hazard, especially with other parties above.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail east onto ledges and talus, crossing the east crest of East Twin Peak, then drop into the boulder fields that fill the 5,300-5,800 ft band. Steep heather benches lead up onto the connecting ridge: stay low on its flank rather than climbing onto the crest, which looks like the line and dead-ends against the upper cliffs. A short 3rd class step gains the wide talus-and-snow field under the cliff band.

waypoints.name: West Chimney crux
waypoints.note: The class 4 chimney regarded as the route's crux: decent footholds but poor handholds; a looser class 3 bypass exists to the right.
waypoints.directions: Keep left of the snow patch that lingers here well into midsummer and work up the loose talus toward the cliff band, then traverse ledges south beneath it around 6,800 ft to find the break. This stretch is where rockfall bites, most of it knocked down by other climbers, so keep the party tight and never directly stacked.

waypoints.name: Columbia Peak
waypoints.note: Hook left/clockwise around the final tower for a short class 3 scramble to the true summit; views of Columbia Glacier, Kyes Peak, and Monte Cristo Peak.
waypoints.directions: Above the break the angle eases back to 3rd class. Follow the west side of the big slabby face over scree-covered slabs, and pass a second short cliff band by a rightward-leaning ramp. A ledge then carries you west and around onto the north side of the tower — crumbly and exposed for a few steps — before the short, solid finish.

waypoints.name: Gorge Creek Overlook pull-off
waypoints.note: Parking pull-off on SR 20 near the Gorge Creek bridge, about 2.6 mi east of Newhalem; cross the highway bridge over Gorge Creek to start the off-trail ascent.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 east from Newhalem about 2.6 miles to the Gorge Creek Overlook pull-off at the bridge. Nothing above the overlook is a numbered or maintained trail, and there is no reliable water past the lower forest, so fill up at Gorge Creek before starting.

waypoints.name: Lower cliff band
waypoints.note: First of two brushy cliff bands on the steep forest ascent; bypass on the right (south) side per the standard line.
waypoints.directions: Cross the footbridge over Gorge Creek, leave the overlook path immediately, and start straight up the forested south-southwest flank on boot-track, cairns and game trails. The lower forest is steep and brushy and partly inside a 2015 burn, so expect deadfall; an animal-path line through the open timber is generally the fastest way through. Near 2,400 ft the first cliff band blocks the fall line — work right around it.

waypoints.name: Upper cliff band
waypoints.note: Second cliff band above the first; stay right through mixed forest and brush to avoid exposed rock.
waypoints.directions: Above the first band the steep timber continues and the second cliff band arrives only about 400 ft higher. Work right again through mixed forest and brush rather than trying to force a line up the rock.

waypoints.name: Vine maple / open timber band
waypoints.note: Route opens into more travelable open timber with vine maple and occasional animal paths after the steep lower forest slog.
waypoints.directions: Keep grinding up steep timber to roughly 3,600-3,800 ft, where a brushy gully and intermittent animal paths lead into more open woods and the travel finally eases. This is the longest and least pleasant stretch of the day and there is no water on it.

waypoints.name: Snow-filled gully
waypoints.note: Partially snow-filled gully marking the transition from forest to the upper talus/snow terrain; can hold snow into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: A couple of hundred feet higher the forest gives out at a gully that commonly holds snow well into midsummer. Early season this is where the axe and crampons come out; later in the year it is bare and loose.

waypoints.name: Talus draw
waypoints.note: Narrow talus draw leading up into the alpine snowfields below the south ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the gully up into a narrow talus draw around 4,500 ft that leads clear of the trees. Granite slabs and alpine snowfields start around 4,800-4,850 ft and the angle eases as the ground flattens onto the crest of the southwest ridge.

waypoints.name: South Davis Saddle
waypoints.note: Broad saddle on the south ridge, about 4.4 hrs from the trailhead; flattest ground on the route for a break or bivy, and the gain point for the summit ridge/buttress.
waypoints.directions: Climb snow and talus up the crest to the broad saddle at about 5,700-5,800 ft. Stay left/north of Point 5,872, the subpeak on the east ridge — its slopes have turned parties back with avalanche-prone snow in shoulder-season conditions. Reckon on 4 to 4.5 hours from the car to here for a fit party.

waypoints.name: Davis Peak
waypoints.note: True summit via Class 2-3 rock buttress with slime-coated slabs near the top and a corniced south ridge crest just below.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the inviting line is the wide-open snow slopes leading to the east summit ridge, and it is a trap: those slopes close out at an impassable step roughly 300 ft below the top, and the retreat costs hours and a thousand feet of regain. Take the rock buttress instead, climbing its right flank — it looks steep and loose from below but goes at Class 2-3. Near the top a short 3rd-class chimney and a band of mossy, slime-coated slabs are the last obstacle, and the slabs can be turned by traversing hard left. The south ridge crest just under the summit can carry a cornice.

waypoints.name: Hairpin Turn pullout (Hwy 20 roadside parking, Washington Pass)
waypoints.note: Roadside pullout at the highway's hairpin switchback just east of Washington Pass; no permit required. This coordinate is the one recorded for Hairpin Crags itself — parking at the hairpin is the entire approach instruction, and there is no separately surveyed parking pin distinct from the crag location.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the roadside pullout at the highway's hairpin switchback just east of Washington Pass and park there; no permit is required. The pullout is the trailhead — from the car it is a short scramble up into the Ice Box, so there is no spur road or further driving.

waypoints.name: Ice Box right side topout
waypoints.note: Corrected coordinate - matches this area's own registered location (Ice Box right side, Hairpin Crags, Washington Pass) and the real Ice Box left side crag used by nearby routes (Iceman, Route C, Route D) in this same database.

waypoints.name: Ice Box right side / Ephemeral base
Ice Box (right side) formation, Hairpin Crags
waypoints.note: Not a distinct mountain summit — a slab/gully rock formation that routes top out on. Elevation is an estimate carried over from the adjacent, similarly-elevationed Ice Box left side (5,490 ft); no separate elevation is recorded for the right side.

waypoints.name: Wolf Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Parking area off Left Fork Wolf Creek Road (FS 5505); Northwest Forest Pass required, no wilderness permit needed.
waypoints.directions: The Wolf Creek Trailhead is a large parking area at the end of FS Road 5505 (Left Fork Wolf Creek Road) above Winthrop, at about 2,900 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required; no wilderness permit is needed. Check current Wolf Creek Road conditions before you drive in. Most parties come mid-July through September, once the trail and the upper basins are snow-free.

waypoints.name: North Fork Wolf Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Crossing of the North Fork — a fire-damaged log bridge, and in early season a difficult, hazardous ford; reliable water here.
waypoints.directions: Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops about 250 ft out of the trailhead, then settles into a long, gently graded valley-bottom walk into the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. Nearly all of this stretch burned in the 2021 Cedar Creek Fire, so expect blackened deadfall, standing dead snags and almost no shade — a real overhead hazard in wind. The North Fork crossing is a couple of miles in and can run high in early season.

waypoints.name: Gardner Meadows
waypoints.note: Three established campsites in fire-cleared, avalanche-scoured meadow terrain along Wolf Creek; the standard basecamp for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Continue straight up the Wolf Creek valley for roughly another eight miles of easy, gradually rising trail, still through burn the whole way. The Abernathy Lake trail splits off around seven and a half miles in — stay on the valley trail. The meadows open out over about a mile; water runs through them and the established camps are here.

waypoints.name: Off-trail turnoff toward the Gardner/North Gardner basin
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Wolf Creek Trail here, staying west of the small stream draining south off Gardner Mountain, and climb toward the basin below the two peaks.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the meadows and start cross-country toward the peak, staying on the west bank of the small stream that drains south off Gardner. Grassy benches lead up to a small meadow basin below the two peaks.

waypoints.name: Scree/talus crux slope
waypoints.note: About 1,400 ft of gain in a half mile of loose, marble-sized scree and sand below the ridge crest — a slow 'one step forward, two steps back' grind.
waypoints.directions: Above the basin the ground turns to loose, marble-sized scree over sand — roughly 1,400 ft of gain in about half a mile, slow going with a faint climber's path that is easy to lose. Into early summer, snow patches linger on this slope and are worth an ice axe.

waypoints.name: Connecting saddle (~7,900 ft)
waypoints.note: Saddle between Gardner and North Gardner where the ridge route to Gardner's summit begins; also the reversal point on descent back down the northwest ridge.
waypoints.directions: Keep grinding up the scree, threading a few short cliff bands and gullies, to top out on the ridge crest. This stretch is the route-finding crux of the approach and the rock underfoot stays loose the whole way.

waypoints.name: Gardner Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Broad, gentle summit on the ridge crest, second-highest peak of the Methow Mountains; open ridge is exposed to lightning in afternoon storms.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle, follow the ridge to the true summit: easier walking on broken rock with occasional hand-holds and brief exposure near the top, class 2-3. The summit is broad and fully open, with no shelter if afternoon storms build.

waypoints.name: Rainy Pass PCT North Trailhead
waypoints.note: A separate, slightly lower trailhead ~1 mi east of Rainy Pass, matching the recorded GPS track for the route.

waypoints.name: Baker River Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 1107022; Northwest Forest Pass required for day parking and a self-issue Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness permit is at the kiosk (confirm current FR 1107 access - a 2025 washout has intermittently closed the road at mile 4).
waypoints.directions: From Sedro-Woolley, follow SR 20 east 16 miles to milepost 82, turn north on Baker Lake Road (FR 11) for 14 miles to Baker Dam Road, cross the Upper Baker Dam, continue 8 miles on FR 1107, then turn onto spur FR 1107022 and follow it to the road-end trailhead. Pavement ends at Baker Dam Road; everything beyond it is gravel Forest Service road.

waypoints.name: Upper Watson Lake
waypoints.note: Corrected coordinate (WA Dept. of Fish & Wildlife high-lakes database) - the previous value was a duplicate of the Hagan Mountain summit, not the lake. Designated backcountry campsites on rock outcroppings along the upper lake with a privy; no campfires allowed - last reliable, easy water before the route goes cross-country.
waypoints.directions: Start on the maintained Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail 611 from the road end. Where the tread splits at about 4,700 ft, take the left (Watson) branch - the right fork drops half a mile to lower Anderson Lake - then climb roughly another half mile to the saddle near 4,800 ft where the trail crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, and descend from it to the lakes at about 4,400 ft. This is the last graded trail on the route; everything above the upper lake is cross-country.

waypoints.name: ~5,300-ft saddle below Mt. Watson
waypoints.note: Cross-country gain point beyond the maintained trail: traverse rock slabs, scree and lingering snowfields beneath Mt. Watson to top this saddle, then drop through heather toward the Diobsud basin.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the upper lake and go cross-country, climbing toward the terminal moraine below Mt. Watson. Traverse rock slabs, scree and lingering snowfields beneath the peak to top the roughly 5,300 ft saddle. There is no tread, no signage and no marked line from here on, so navigate deliberately with map and compass or GPS rather than expecting to follow anything.

waypoints.name: Uppermost Diobsud Lake
waypoints.note: Established rough camp in the upper Diobsud Lakes basin used as a staging point before continuing north toward the Bacon-Hagan saddle; roughly 6 hours of travel from the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the saddle through open heather and easy slopes into the Diobsud basin, aiming for the uppermost pair of the four Diobsud Lakes. Heather and open ground with route-finding required, but no technical terrain. On-file timing puts this camp at roughly 6 to 6.5 hours and about 7.4 miles from the trailhead, with around 3,600 ft of gain and 500 ft of loss, and it is the standard base for the south-slopes climb.

waypoints.name: Hidden Lake (Bacon-Hagan saddle)
waypoints.note: Small unofficial-name tarn in the low saddle between Bacon Peak and Hagan Mountain, draining to Hidden Creek; reliable water and a flat-enough bivy if needed.

waypoints.name: Cliff-band forest slopes, south flank of Hagan
waypoints.note: Steep bushwhack north through timber past two cliff bands to break out onto open heather and grass on Hagan's south side - the most sustained brush/route-finding crux of the approach.
waypoints.directions: From the tarn, bushwhack north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliff bands - this is the sustained route-finding crux of the whole approach. Pick brushy ramps and weaknesses through each band to keep the ground climbable; above them the timber breaks out onto open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank around 6,000-6,400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. Mark your line through the bands with photos, cairns or a GPS track before going higher: the descent reverses this exact ground, the weaknesses you threaded coming up are hard to spot from above, and the descent is consistently reported as slower and more error-prone than the climb.

waypoints.name: Scree/talus couloir col, SW end of Hagan
waypoints.note: Ascend a broad, loose scree-and-talus couloir to a col near the southwest end of the summit crags; this is the same col the descent down-climbs back to the heather benches - watch for rockfall onto parties below.
waypoints.directions: From the heather benches, ascend a broad talus-and-scree couloir to a col near the southwest end of the Hagan summit crags, around 7,000 ft. The couloir is loose the whole way - helmets on, and keep the party either tight together or well spread out rather than stacked, since anything kicked here runs straight onto whoever is below. This is the same col the descent downclimbs back to the benches.

waypoints.name: Hagan Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scrambling up slabs from the col to the summit ridge; several rocky bumps along the crest, so identify the true high point before topping out.
waypoints.directions: From the col at the southwest end of the crags, make a rising, crevasse- and moat-aware traverse around the ice apron of the Hagan Glacier to reach the second col, the one between Hagan's twin summits. This short glacier section is the technical crux of the route despite the Class 2-3 billing: carry rope, harness and a crevasse-rescue kit, and put crampons on - on-file guidance recommends both even in midsummer, and although one published party crossed the upper glacier unroped, a single trip report is not the standard. The moat is the same hazard in both directions on the way back. From the twin-summit col a short Class 2-3 scramble on slabs gains the summit ridge. Hagan carries several rocky bumps of similar height along that crest, so identify the true high point (7,067-7,080 ft depending on source) before committing to the last moves.

waypoints.name: Tye Road / Old Stevens Pass Highway pullout (near double hairpin turn, ~1.4 mi from US 2)
waypoints.note: Same approach as all other Half Moon Crag routes; see wa_artic_rose note on coordinate precision.
waypoints.directions: Take US-2 east out of Seattle or Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway, now signed Tye Road, which runs toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite. Follow it roughly 1.4 miles from US-2 and park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn.

waypoints.name: Half Moon Crag
waypoints.note: Granite crag visible from Highway 2, ~45-60min/1,000ft approach through old-growth forest. Routes are short (≤85 ft), so this single coordinate serves as both approach reference and topout.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Old roadbed starts at the Goodell Creek group campground turnout off SR 20 (milepost 119) near Newhalem; self-issue wilderness permit required for overnight, Northwest Forest Pass for day parking.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 about 60 miles - roughly an hour and a half - east from Burlington and park at the Goodell Creek Campground turnout at milepost 119, just west of Newhalem. The highway is paved all the way to here, and the trailhead sits west of both of SR 20's winter closure gates (Ross Dam at milepost 134, and Newhalem at milepost 120 in harder winters), so driving access to this trailhead does not depend on the seasonal opening of the highway east of the park.

waypoints.name: Roadbed End / Basin Fork
waypoints.note: The 4-mile old roadbed peters out at a stone cairn in a wide clearing; the defined path forks right toward Terror Creek Basin, while a fainter boot path continues straight for the Crescent Creek Basin / Stump Hollow approach used for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and Frenzel Spitz.
waypoints.directions: Follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed upstream along the true left (south) side of Goodell Creek. It is grassy and gravelly, flat and easy walking for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet from the ~600 ft trailhead to about 1,700-1,800 ft. The end of it is not obvious from the tread - watch on the right, in the wide clearing, for the cairn or stone marker climbers call the 'stone arrow', which is what marks the unsigned climbers' path leaving the creek bottom.

waypoints.name: Treeline Breakout
waypoints.note: Boot path breaks out of old-growth forest onto steep heather benches and slab; the steep, brushy tread above the roadbed is easy to lose in fog.
waypoints.directions: Top off water at Goodell Creek before leaving the roadbed: there is none reliable again until treeline. From the cairn, the boot path leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply up into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow. Expect steep root-and-duff footing with slide alder and devil's club low down; the path stays reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher up, but multiple trip reports on this approach describe losing it, and it is especially easy to lose in fog - track it deliberately rather than trusting the tread to hold. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the timber gives way to the heather benches and slab of Stump Hollow, a slabby basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block.

waypoints.name: Terror-Crescent Divide Saddle
waypoints.note: Rising traverse gains this ~6,200 ft saddle on the ridge dividing Terror Creek and Crescent Creek basins; drop west off the saddle into Crescent Creek Basin from here.
waypoints.directions: From Stump Hollow, make a rising traverse over meadow, slab and - early to mid season - snow to the broad saddle at roughly 6,200 ft on the Barrier, the ridge dividing Terror Creek basin from Crescent Creek basin. Carry an ice axe for this, and crampons early season.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin Streams
waypoints.note: Two snowmelt streams run off the slabs above camp; reliable early-to-mid season but reported to thin out by late August in dry years.
waypoints.directions: This leg is the Barrier crossing, the most exposed piece of the approach and one of the route's named hazards. Cross by one of two options: a lower line on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher line over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mt. Degenhardt. Either takes under an hour, but both are loose enough that rockfall onto anyone below is the real hazard - helmets on, and do not stack the party. Drop the far (west) side of the saddle into Crescent Creek Basin, where two snowmelt streams run off the slabs; they are reliable early to mid season but reported to thin out by late August in dry years, so plan your water around that rather than assuming they run.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Established gravel-and-heather camp on slabs used as the base for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and Frenzel Spitz; reach it via the stump-hollow traverse rather than the Terror Basin path.
waypoints.directions: A last short step across the gravel and heather slabs from the stream draws to the established basin camp at roughly 5,800 ft below Mt. Terror. This is the standard base for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn and Frenzel Spitz, and it is reached by the Stump Hollow traverse rather than by the Terror Basin path. Camping here is at-large with no designated sites, but an NPS backcountry permit is required for the overnight, and a park-wide moratorium bans new fixed anchors - plan on clean, removable gear for everything above.

waypoints.name: Himmel-Otto Col Gully
waypoints.note: Narrow gully gains the Himmel-Otto col between Himmelhorn and Ottohorn; straightforward snow early season, but by late season expect icy neve, chossy moats, and an overhanging boulder near the top forcing a loose class 3/4 bypass on climber's left.
waypoints.directions: From camp, climb the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto col between Himmelhorn and Ottohorn. What this leg actually is depends entirely on season. Early, it is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top: axe, and crampons if it has firmed up. Late, the same gully is icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col commonly forces a loose, exposed Class 3-4 bypass on the climber's left. Coming back down late season, parties often find fixed or placed rappel anchors in the moat sections more trustworthy than downclimbing loose rock alongside hard snow - there are no bolted stations anywhere on this route, so carry slings, cord and tat to build your own.

waypoints.name: Himmelhorn Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (7,880 ft); the Southeast Route finishes via crack systems on the face above the col — downclimb and rappel the same line back to the Himmel-Otto col to descend.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the 23-mile Cascade River Road out of Marblemount; NPS wilderness permit (with bear canister for overnight) required, no day-use fee inside the park.
waypoints.directions: The final miles of Cascade River Road out of Marblemount are unpaved and washboarded, and high clearance or AWD makes the drive to the road end considerably easier.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass and turns east toward Pelton/Horseshoe Basin; a signed spur drops 1 mi and 800 ft to Doubtful Lake below the Sahale Arm.
waypoints.directions: Take the Cascade Pass Trail's well-graded switchbacks up the valley headwall, about 1,800 ft of gain on the only fully maintained tread of the route. Everything above the pass is unmaintained, loose and cairn-marked by comparison, so cover this section efficiently.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.note: Highest established backcountry camp in the park, at the base of Sahale Glacier; wind-wall rock sites, reservable NPS permit required, snowmelt water only early season.
waypoints.directions: Continue past the pass junction onto the Sahale Arm Trail and climb the open heather ridge, passing the Doubtful Lake overlook, to the camp at the toe of the glacier. It is a steady 2,200 ft of exposed, shadeless climbing with no water until you reach camp.

waypoints.name: Secret Gully descent off Sahale Arm
waypoints.note: Climbers' descent gully dropping east off the Sahale Arm into Horseshoe Basin; loose rock on slabs and unstable underfoot once snow-free.
waypoints.directions: From camp, traverse east across the boulder-and-heather plateau below the glacier, passing the dozen or so established camp pads, then downclimb a steep snowfield that can stay firm or icy into midsummer — an axe or whippet earns its place here. Traverse east again to gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge, then follow the cairned climbers' trail down the ridge over one short 4th-class step to where the gully drops away east.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Basin staging area
waypoints.note: Waterfall-lined cirque beneath Ripsaw Ridge between Boston Peak and Buckner; stage here before the scramble up to Horseshoe Peak's south-facing gully.
waypoints.directions: Descend the scree-and-talus gully to the snowfield at about 6,600 ft and cross it into the basin. Melted out, the gully is loose mostly-3rd-class ground that needs real care; with snow still in it the concern shifts to steep firm snow instead. In the basin, traverse the wide ledge at roughly 6,600 ft as it rises toward the ruins of the old Black Warrior mine near 6,800 ft. Do not drink the basin's water — it drains historic mine tailings, so carry what you need from Doubtful Creek or camp.

waypoints.name: Summit gully and ledge
waypoints.note: 30-45° loose gully climbs to a ledge about 100 ft below the true summit, directly below the final 5.2 notch.
waypoints.directions: Contour northeast and then east on loose scree, talus and slabs below the Davenport Glacier to reach the base of Ripsaw Ridge under the peak, then start up the Class 3 dike-and-gully system. A short Class 4 step breaks it partway up. The whole line is loose enough that another party above you is the main hazard, so wear a helmet and keep the group either tight or well out of the fall line.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Peak
waypoints.note: True summit gained by ~5 ft of 5th-class climbing to a one-meter-square notch (feels overhung but isn't); downclimb or single-rope rappel to reverse.
waypoints.directions: From the ledge, scramble about 10 ft of Class 3/4 onto a ledge that angles diagonally up the south face to an obvious cleft just below the top, exiting on loose Class 3/4 rock at the notch. The final moves are 5.2 over fall-would-be-fatal exposure, so most parties rope the ramp as one pitch of roughly 30 m and belay off the horn on the east side of the notch. That horn is also the rappel anchor on the way down; it is natural rock with no fixed hardware, so carry a few cams in case the sling is missing or worn.

waypoints.name: Lightning Creek boat landing / trail junction
waypoints.note: Water-taxi drop point on Ross Lake's east shore (~10 lake-miles north of Ross Dam); pick up the East Bank/Lightning Creek Trail here — this is mile ~16 of the SR-20 approach trail, a designated boat-in camp requiring a backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Willow Lake
waypoints.note: Small lake along the trail (~mile 20); last reliable water before leaving the maintained trail — the 1988 southeast-buttress party left the trail just beyond Willow Lake to cut east toward the peak.

waypoints.name: Off-trail brush/ravine to the 5,000-ft shoulder
waypoints.note: Cross-country push through timber and avalanche debris into a deep ravine, then steep dirt-and-brush climbing to a broad timbered shoulder and meadows near 5,000 ft, bypassing cliff bands on their west side.

waypoints.name: 6,200-ft saddle below the SE buttress
waypoints.note: Ridge saddle directly beneath the southeast buttress, used as a bivouac by the 1988 first-ascent party; no reported water — carry up from Willow Lake.

waypoints.name: Southeast buttress — loose rock / crux chimney
waypoints.note: Divided buttress climbing on often loose, friable rock (hard hat mandatory, protection scarce); crux is a steep chimney (5.6) low on the buttress, followed by a 50° dihedral and a loose upper gully.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20) / East Bank Trail to Lightning Creek
waypoints.note: This is a long (~15+ mile) approach via the East Bank Trail, historically used for this specific technical route; most modern non-technical South Peak trip reports instead use the shorter Hozomeen Lake Trailhead at Hozomeen Campground (Silver-Skagit Road, from the Canadian side)

waypoints.name: Hannegan Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-32 (5.3 mi off Hannegan Pass Road); day-use fee/Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk and no potable water is available at this site.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of FS Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road), which turns off SR 542, the Mt. Baker Highway, at about 3,100 feet. A day-use fee or Northwest Forest Pass is required at the trailhead kiosk, and there is no potable water available at the trailhead itself.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Camp
waypoints.note: Signed spur camp about a half mile below the pass with a food-storage cache and vault toilet; no reliable running water past this point.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Trail junction with the Hannegan Peak, Copper Ridge, and Chilliwack trails; leave the maintained trail here and climb the dusty gully south toward Ruth Mountain's ridge.

waypoints.name: Ruth Glacier toe / heather ridge
waypoints.note: Climbers' path skirts a minor peak on a heather-filled ridge before dropping onto the lowest snow finger of the Ruth Glacier, usually crampon-free on this well-covered lower section.

waypoints.name: Ruth Mountain summit bivy
waypoints.note: Common two-day bivy spot near Ruth's true summit (not the benchmark) before continuing to Icy Peak; flat tent sites with seasonal snowmelt for water.

waypoints.name: Ruth-Icy col descent
waypoints.note: Descend talus and snowfields off Ruth's south ridge to the saddle; avoid the steep 'death gully' variant in favor of the cairned heather slopes to climber's left.

waypoints.name: Icy Glacier crevasse traverse
waypoints.note: Rope up here to cross the Icy Glacier's northwest slope; crevasses lie mostly downhill to climber's right, so keep the rock ridge on your left.

waypoints.name: Icy Peak summit
waypoints.note: Class 4 gully with real exposure gains the summit; rappel or downclimb the same ~100 ft gully off slings around a rock horn to descend.

waypoints.name: Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (Trail #96)
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk (no fee); Northwest Forest Pass or National Park Pass required to park, with an overflow lot at nearby Berry Patch Trailhead.

waypoints.name: Goat Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford of Goat Creek on the Snowgrass Trail in forest cover; a reliable water source about 2 miles in.

waypoints.name: Lower Snowgrass Flat / Lily Basin Trail (#86) junction
waypoints.note: Established campsites near the Lily Basin Trail junction; a spring at the head of Snowgrass Creek (about a quarter mile off-trail) is the last dependable water before the ridge.

waypoints.name: Pacific Crest Trail junction
waypoints.note: Snowgrass Trail meets the PCT; head north toward Old Snowy Mountain to reach the Ives approach ridge.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy - Ives col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak where the north ridge route onto Ives begins; also the top of the Class 1-2 northwest ridge used on the descent.

waypoints.name: Southwest face ramp traverse
waypoints.note: Drop off the ridge crest onto a loose ramp and traverse roughly 40 ft climber's right below the summit cliff; exposed Class 3 terrain, loose underfoot.

waypoints.name: Ives Peak summit
waypoints.note: Broad rocky true summit (7,920+ ft) with views of Mt. Adams, Mt. Rainier, and the McCall Glacier on the northeast face.

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue free Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead register; $5 day-use/Northwest Forest Pass required for the SR-20 lot near Granite/Canyon Creek.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR-20, roughly 16 miles west of Rainy Pass at about 1,900 feet. The lot takes a $5 day-use fee or a Northwest Forest Pass, and there is a register at the trailhead where you self-issue the free Pasayten Wilderness permit. If you are camping, the high camps fall inside the North Cascades park complex and Ross Lake NRA backcountry, so arrange a wilderness camping permit before you leave. The route is usually climbed August into September.

waypoints.name: Jackita Ridge Trail / Crater Lake Trail fork
waypoints.note: Trail #738 switchbacks ~3,400 ft in 4 miles (about 55 switchbacks) to this fork; leave Jackita Ridge Trail and go left for Crater Lake.
waypoints.directions: Cross Canyon Creek on the log-and-plank crossing right at the start; it can wash out in high water, so check its condition before committing to the trip. Above it the trail settles into roughly fifty switchbacks and about 3,400 ft of forested climbing over four miles. Carry water from the creek, because the hillside above holds none.

waypoints.name: Crater Lake
waypoints.note: Grade flattens around 5,000 ft at the lake basin; campsites sit on the rocky south lip and the outlet is the last reliable water before cross-country travel toward Jerry Lakes.
waypoints.directions: Bear left at the fork and contour about a mile into the lake basin, losing a little height as the grade finally eases — the only downhill on the way in.

waypoints.name: Crater Mountain south saddle
waypoints.note: Cross-country ridge-gain point above Crater Lake where the trail ends and the route drops off-trail toward the Jerry Glacier remnant.
waypoints.directions: Pick the trail back up above the lake and grind out roughly 2,200 ft of long, hot, exposed switchbacks with no water on any of them. Somewhere around 6,700-7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse off toward the gap between Crater Mountain's main summit and its east peak. Most parties are a little over four hours from the car when they reach it.

waypoints.name: Jerry Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Small crevassed glacier below the saddle; trip reports describe roping up or using crampons to descend safely toward Jerry Lakes.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the route goes downhill onto the ice on the far side. Early in the season the glacier is snow-covered and crevassed enough to justify a rope and crampons; by late summer it is often patchy or nearly bare, which makes the crossing simpler but the consequences of a slide worse.

waypoints.name: Jerry Lakes / Crater Creek Meadows camp
waypoints.note: Established bench camp near Jerry Lakes reached roughly 8-8.5 hrs from the trailhead; standard bivy for a South Face summit push the next morning.
waypoints.directions: Continue down off the ice into the lakes basin, losing around 800 ft over heather, slabs and boulders with no set line to follow. Fill water at the lakes: this is the last of it before the face.

waypoints.name: Hidden chimney / red gully, South Face
waypoints.note: Class-3 hidden chimney cuts the lower cliff band above a fish-shaped snowfield and a slinged rappel boulder; loose rock, a short rappel, and exposed steep snow through here.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the heather shelf out of the basin and through the notch just south of the lakes, then climb easily to a level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,200 ft. From there make a rising traverse on scree westward beneath the face to the snow patches under its lower cliff band, often moving in the shallow moat where the snow has pulled away from the rock. Those snowfields are steep enough to want crampons late in the season, and the break in the cliff band above them stays hidden until you are almost underneath it.

waypoints.name: Jack Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a notch just west of the summit blocks followed by a short, exposed class-3 finish.
waypoints.directions: Above the cliff band the face gives 400-500 ft of class 3 ramps and ledges strung together by harder class 4 steps and traverses, then eases into straightforward scrambling and a band of scree beside a snow patch that returns you to the southeast ridge near 8,600 ft. Traverse and drop slightly to get in under the summit cliffs, then take the partly snow-filled gully above at class 3 and 4 with one step that can feel low fifth. Holds pull off freely on all of it, so keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked in the gully.

waypoints.name: Hairpin Turn Pullout (SR-20)
waypoints.note: Park in the large plowed turnout at the hairpin switchback on SR-20, ~1 mi downhill/east of Washington Pass; no permit or Northwest Forest Pass required.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the Hairpin Turn pullout, about one mile east of Washington Pass at roughly 5,150 feet — a large, plowed turnout right at the switchback. No permit or Northwest Forest Pass is required to park there. Keep in mind SR-20 over Washington Pass is gated in winter and typically doesn't reopen until late April or May, so early-season parties should expect lingering snow on the approach.

waypoints.name: Climbers Path into Boulder Field
waypoints.note: Head south off the highway into timber on a lightly worn, sometimes-hard-to-follow path; after about a quarter mile it joins the main cairned climbers trail.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Reached in roughly 1 hour from the car at the head of the Early Winters Creek basin; drop about 20 ft below the pass to pick up the climbers trail hugging the slabs toward the Notch.

waypoints.name: Notch Below Little Finger
waypoints.note: Gully leads up to the notch between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; this is the start of the North Face route and where the rope typically goes on.

waypoints.name: Pitch 1 Loose Rock (Angled Crack)
waypoints.note: P1 climbs up and left through an angled crack on rock reported as loose near its start; belayer should stay out of the fall line and watch for kicked debris.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Temple Summit
waypoints.note: Detached granite tower on Wallaby Peak's SE ridge; descend via three single 60m rappels from chains atop the North Face and at the P1 belay.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: FS Trail 677 off Glacier Creek Rd (FS-39); Northwest Forest Pass or digital day-use pass required at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Fast, rock-hopped crossing that worsens with afternoon snowmelt; real injuries have happened here — cross early in the day.
waypoints.directions: Trail #677 leaves the lot and climbs steadily through old growth, the lower creeks bridged and no junctions to think about for the first couple of miles. The grade is relentless but it is plain walking; on the pre-dawn start this route needs, it is the stretch you cover in the dark.

waypoints.name: Kulshan Cabin site
waypoints.note: Established camp at the old 1925 Kulshan Cabin site, just before the signed Climbers' Trail junction.
waypoints.directions: A short, steepening 0.2 mi carries on through thinning forest to the flat bench where the cabin stood, with a backcountry toilet as the obvious landmark. That toilet and the one at Harrison Camp are the only ones on this side — everything above here is pack-it-out.

waypoints.name: Hogsback moraine camp
waypoints.note: Climbers' Trail switchbacks up the Hogsback moraine crest to a common high camp just below the Coleman Glacier toe.
waypoints.directions: Just past the cabin site the trail reaches a well-signed fork: take the right branch, the Climbers' Trail. The left branch is the hikers' continuation toward the Heliotrope Ridge viewpoint and is the common wrong turn here. The right fork gains roughly 1,000 ft in about a mile, steep and direct up the moraine crest.

waypoints.name: Coleman Glacier toe / rope-up point
waypoints.note: Rope up here for glacier travel; crevasse hazard increases traversing beneath the Black Buttes cirque toward Lincoln Peak.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the moraine crest above camp as it narrows and runs out at the glacier's edge, another ~1,000 ft over about half a mile. Footing is loose rock and sand on the crest, and the ground turns to ice and rubble where the moraine meets the toe.

waypoints.name: Black Buttes basin camp
waypoints.note: High camp used for Black Buttes objectives, tucked below the Buttes off the standard Coleman Glacier line.
waypoints.directions: From the toe the travel is roped glacier across to the 7,200 ft bench beneath the Black Buttes. The line passes under serac bands on the Coleman's icefall, so it is a stretch to keep moving through rather than rest in, and it wants crossing early while the glacier is still frozen — timing matters more on this side than on the peak's southwest approach.

waypoints.name: NW Face start / hanging glacier icefall
waypoints.note: Same start as Assassin Spire's Shooting Gallery route: a 60m WI4 pitch right of a prominent hanging glacier — icefall and rockfall exposure.

waypoints.name: Lincoln Peak summit
waypoints.note: Rime-covered summit ridge gains the top; descend via the SW face (snow/ice to 65°) rather than reversing the NW Face.
waypoints.directions: The ground above the base is roped ice and mixed climbing, not a snow slog: a 60 m WI4 pitch immediately right of the hanging glacier is the technical crux, after which parties simul-climb across the upper amphitheater basin. Above that expect roughly four more roped pitches on steeper ice separated by snowfields up to 70 degrees, finishing on rime-plastered ridge and an icy chimney. The rock off the ice is rotten volcanic choss with no fixed gear, so anchors come off slung horns and blocks and every one of them should be treated as suspect.

waypoints.name: Lincoln Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit.

waypoints.name: FR-9070 / PCT (#2000) junction near Olallie Meadow, Snoqualmie Pass
waypoints.note: Where FR-9070 crosses the PCT: from I-90 exit 54, Hyak Drive NE becomes FR-9070 and runs 5.4 mi to this crossing. Past the junction, climbers take the LEFT fork of FR-9070 and drive or walk to a large turnaround just below Silver Basin, from which the crag base is a 20-30 min approach on foot. That turnaround has no published name or coordinate, so this junction is the closest fixed reference point rather than the exact parking spot.
waypoints.directions: Leave I-90 at Exit 54 (Hyak) and follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, staying on it past the end of the pavement for about 5.4 miles to the Ollallie Meadow junction where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and keep driving until the road ends in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin; that turnaround is where you park, and the pin here marks the PCT crossing rather than the road end itself. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from about July through November.

waypoints.name: The Obelisk (rock formation/crag), Silver Basin
waypoints.note: Elevation is an estimate from the surrounding terrain (Citidel base area is listed at 4,585 ft; The Obelisk sits further up-slope from the Sofa King Buttress sub-area, per MP's own text) — MP does not publish a separate elevation figure for this formation.

waypoints.name: Monument Creek Trailhead (Lost River Road / Harts Pass Road)
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead on Lost River Road (FR 5400 spur); Northwest Forest Pass or self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk, last reliable water/toilet before miles of Pasayten trail.

waypoints.name: Robinson Pass
waypoints.note: Gains the Middle Fork Pasayten divide via a steep final 1.2-mile forested pitch; trail forks here toward the Pasayten River valley.
waypoints.directions: Trail #478 follows Robinson Creek through big timber for about six miles, never far from the sound of the water, then fords the creek. Above the ford the grade stays gradual through forest, crossing several avalanche runouts, and breaks into meadowland near 4,700 ft. Pass the Slate Pass Trail junction and finish with a half mile of open meadow climbing to the pass.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten River flats
waypoints.note: Common first-night camp beside the river a few miles below Robinson Pass; reliable water but mosquito-heavy in early season.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and descend about three miles into the broad U-shaped Middle Fork valley, losing roughly 1,800 ft to river level. Camps sit along the water here.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.note: Green alpine lake ringed by larches with a popular established camp; last dependable water before the Rolo/Shellrock high country.
waypoints.directions: Continue down-river before the trail turns and climbs back into the high country, gaining around 2,100 ft to the lake basin. Fred's Lake sits a short way off the main trail rather than on it, so watch for the spur or you will walk straight past it.

waypoints.name: Rolo Pass
waypoints.note: Ridge-crest pass just above Fred's Lake; route continues cross-country toward the head of Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin.
waypoints.directions: From the lake keep climbing to the ridge-crest pass a few hundred feet above, through open larch and talus. The maintained tread thins out above the lake, and this is where the route stops being a trail hike.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Pass / Shellrock Basin
waypoints.note: Trail here has been unmaintained for decades and the basin fogs in frequently; easy to lose the faint tread in whiteout, navigate by map/compass.
waypoints.directions: From Rolo Pass drop to the headwaters of Eureka Creek and traverse across into Shellrock Basin, then climb to the pass at 7,500 ft. The tread through here has been unmaintained for decades and is faint to nonexistent, and the basin fogs in readily — carry map and compass and be ready to navigate without seeing any of the surrounding peaks.

waypoints.name: Lost Peak
waypoints.note: Class 3 talus/meadow scramble up the southwest or northwest ridge from a Shellrock Pass area camp; descend the same ridge line reversed.
waypoints.directions: From a camp near the pass, gain either the southwest or the northwest ridge and follow it over talus and alpine meadow to the top. Class 3 with no sustained technical ground, but the crest is high, exposed to wind, and can hold snow well past midsummer.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road's-end trailhead on Cascade River Road (23.1 mi gravel from Marblemount); NPS wilderness permit required for camps beyond Cascade Pass.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), about 23.1 miles of gravel road from Marblemount, at roughly 3,600 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here. Overnight parties also need a North Cascades backcountry camping permit for Kool-Aid Lake, picked up in person in Marblemount before you drive out.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail tops out here; leave it for the unmaintained climber's path bearing SSE toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: The Cascade Pass Trail is well-graded and heavily switchbacked the whole way, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft to the notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. It melts out by early to mid summer and is the busiest stretch of the trip, since it is a popular day hike in its own right. Nothing here needs route-finding; the work starts at the pass.

waypoints.name: Cache Glacier toe / Mixup Peak traverse
waypoints.note: Rising traverse on snow or heather across Mixup Peak's east flank to the base of Cache Glacier; isolated crevasses and firm morning snow can require an axe.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on Mixup Peak's east flank. The path is intermittent and vanishes entirely under early-season snow, so this is where navigation starts to matter. It brings you to the toe of the Cache Glacier around 6,000 ft, where firm morning snow makes an ice axe worth its weight.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Glaciated gap atop Cache Glacier between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak; descend SSE from here toward Kool-Aid Lake.
waypoints.directions: Ascend the glacier on moderate snow, steepening to about 35 degrees near the top, to reach the col. This glacier is small and generally free of significant crevasse hazard, but it is still a snow slope with runout below, so crampons are worth carrying depending on season and how firm it is.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn with established bivy sites used as base camp for the peak; outlet is snowbound and unreliable for water into early summer.
waypoints.directions: From the col the route drops rather than climbs: a climber's path makes a descending traverse to the southeast down to the lake. Do not continue north over the col. This is the last reliable water of the trip, and the outlet can still be snowbound into early summer, so fill here before going up.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain–Hurry-up Peak col
waypoints.note: Climb roughly 1,000 ft from Kool-Aid Lake to this saddle, then gain Magic Mountain's south ridge toward the false summit.
waypoints.directions: From the lake the ground turns up again onto heather and scree leading east to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, where the South Ridge proper begins. There is no water at all above the lake, so leave camp carrying what you need. The slope is uniform and featureless in cloud, which is the only real navigational catch on this leg.

waypoints.name: Corkscrew ledges below false summit
waypoints.note: Past the false summit, drop about 80 ft down a loose gully to exposed Class 3-4 ledges that corkscrew the east side of the peak; a hand line or short belay is often used here.
waypoints.directions: Follow the South Ridge up on heather and rock at class 3 to a false summit, roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true one. Do not try to stay on the crest from there. Drop about 50-80 ft down a loose, dirty gully on the far side to reach the ledge system, which is the technical crux of the whole outing.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit, marking the northern terminus of the Ptarmigan Traverse on the North Cascades NP / Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary.
waypoints.directions: The ledges are broken, exposed class 3-4 and corkscrew around the east side of the summit tower to the top. A hand line or a short belay is commonly used, and many parties rappel this section on the way down off a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there is no fixed hardware on this summit. Fresh snow can force a detour through the moat, and the loose rock means this section bites harder on the descent than on the way up.

waypoints.name: Killen Creek Trailhead #113
waypoints.note: Muddy Meadows is the more specific, closer approach for the northeast glacier cluster (Lava/Lyman/Wilson/Rusk).

waypoints.name: Boulder Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: Boulder Ridge Trail #605 off Baker Lake Rd/FS 1130/1131.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road)
waypoints.note: Sol Duc trailhead at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road, the start of the High Divide / Bailey Range approach. This REPLACES a pin naming Whiskey Bend, 11.7 mi away on the Elwha, which approaches Mount Barnes from the opposite end and never passes Heart Lake — the first waypoint here. Every recorded distance on this route is consistent with a Sol Duc start. Coordinate from published sources rather than the Park Service, which does not publish one.

waypoints.name: Heart Lake
waypoints.note: Last reliable water and common camp before crossing High Divide; trip reports warn there is no water again until well past the Catwalk toward Eleven Bull Basin.

waypoints.name: High Divide crest near Bogachiel Peak
waypoints.note: Maintained High Divide Trail tops out here; this is where the Bailey Range Traverse leaves the trail and drops off-trail east into Cat Basin toward Cat Peak. The exact off-trail departure point is not recorded separately, so this marker sits on the peak itself.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk (Cat Peak-Mt. Carrie arete)
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed ridgeline with a few scrambling moves and roughly 3,000 ft of air to the valley floor; poorly defined in fog, not a place to be in wind or wet rock.

waypoints.name: Upper Ferry Basin / Ferry Glacial Lake
waypoints.note: Open meadow below Mount Ferry with glacial lakes and streams for the last dependable water before the Bear Pass approach; established informal camp used by most Bailey Range parties.

waypoints.name: Childs Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Small glacier/permanent snowfield below Bear Pass; parties report needing ice axe and microspikes on firm snow, with crevasse-type terrain in Junkyard Basin just beyond.

waypoints.name: Bear Pass
waypoints.note: Broad saddle marking the southeastern terminus of the Bailey Range proper; from here the route drops toward a flat meadow before angling southeast for the final Barnes approach.

waypoints.name: Slate Peak Trailhead (Buckskin Ridge TH)
waypoints.note: End of Slate Peak Road (FR-5400), a high-clearance gravel spur off Harts Pass Road; self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk, road typically open only July-September.

waypoints.name: Slate Pass
waypoints.note: Saddle on Buckskin Ridge where the Buckskin Ridge/Middle Fork Pasayten trail junction is reached (~30 min from the TH) and the route leaves the ridge crest to drop steeply toward the West/Middle Fork Pasayten River.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.note: Small subalpine lake with limited established sites reached via a climbing traverse off the Eureka Creek trail; standard first-night base camp for the Carru-Lago-Osceola cluster (~5 hrs in from the trailhead).

waypoints.name: Rolo Pass (ridge crest above Fred's Lake)
waypoints.note: Switchbacks out of the Fred's Lake basin gain this open ridge crest; views back northwest to Fred's Lake and east into the Eureka Creek headwater basin, the divide crossing point toward Shellrock Basin.

waypoints.name: Upper Eureka Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Rock-hop the Eureka Creek headwaters below Rolo Pass before climbing back up into Shellrock Basin; last reliable water before the summit day.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Basin
waypoints.note: Open meadow/talus basin near Shellrock Pass with tarn water, used as the high camp for Carru, Lago, and Blackcap summit pushes.

waypoints.name: Lago-Carru saddle
waypoints.note: Broad col between Mount Lago and Mount Carru; leave the basin here and gain Carru's southeast slope/ridge for the final scramble.

waypoints.name: Mount Carru
waypoints.note: True summit via class 2-3 talus and short rock on the southeast ridge; exposure enough on the final blocks to keep it interesting.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road-end at Hannegan Campground off Ruth Creek Rd/FR-32; Northwest Forest Pass required, self-issue wilderness permit needed for NOCA camps ahead.
waypoints.directions: Drive to the road-end at Hannegan Campground, at the end of FS Road 32 (Ruth Creek Road) off WA-542 — this is the Hannegan Pass Trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here, and a self-issue wilderness permit is needed for the North Cascades National Park camps ahead on the route.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass then drops roughly 650 ft per mile into North Cascades National Park toward the Chilliwack River, the gateway from Mt. Baker Wilderness into the park backcountry.

waypoints.name: Boundary Camp
waypoints.note: Marks the Mt. Baker National Forest / North Cascades National Park boundary; established campsites with pit toilet at the bottom of the roughly 2,500 ft descent off Hannegan Pass.

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River ford / Easy Ridge climbers' path
waypoints.note: Faint, unsigned climbers' path leaves the valley trail here to gain Easy Ridge; parties commonly lose it near the river crossing, especially in fog.

waypoints.name: Whatcom Pass
waypoints.note: High alpine pass on the Chilliwack River/Brush Creek trail (USGS Mount Redoubt quad); the Tapto Lakes side trail branches here while the climbing route continues toward Whatcom Peak and Perfect Pass.

waypoints.name: Perfect Pass
waypoints.note: Renowned high bivy site reached by descending roughly 1,000 ft off Easy Ridge around the exposed 'Imperfect Impasse' notch below Whatcom Peak; last reliable camp before the glacier.

waypoints.name: Challenger Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Crevassed glacier traverse on Challenger's north/northwest slopes from Perfect Pass; crampons recommended even when an existing boot pack is present in season.

waypoints.name: Mount Challenger (East Summit)
waypoints.note: 3rd/4th-class scramble off the glacier exits onto a short 5.6-5.7 pitch to the true east summit; descend by downclimbing to the notch and making a single rappel.

waypoints.name: Staircase Ranger Station
waypoints.note: Approach via Flapjack Lakes Trail to Gladys Divide/Needle Pass. Note: Staircase area is currently closed post-2025 Bear Gulch Fire.

waypoints.name: Staircase Ranger Station
waypoints.note: Approach via Flapjack Lakes Trail to Gladys Divide/Needle Pass. Note: Staircase area is currently closed post-2025 Bear Gulch Fire.

waypoints.name: Phelps Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road-end trailhead off FR 6211 (Chiwawa River Road); no Northwest Forest Pass required here — sign the self-issue register before starting up Phelps Creek Trail #1511.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Chiwawa River Road (FR-62) to the Phelps Creek Road spur, FR 6211, and follow it to its end at the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft). The road typically opens with spring snowmelt by June. No Northwest Forest Pass is required here, but sign the self-issue register before starting up Phelps Creek Trail #1511.

waypoints.name: Glacier Peak Wilderness Boundary
waypoints.note: Phelps Creek Trail crosses into Glacier Peak Wilderness here; trail remains flat and forested for another mile before the Leroy Creek turnoff.

waypoints.name: Leroy Creek Crossing / Leroy High Route Junction
waypoints.note: Ford Leroy Creek and leave the maintained trail here for the unmaintained climbers' path, which switchbacks steeply up the creek's north side — last reliable, easy water before the basin.

waypoints.name: Leroy Basin
waypoints.note: Well-established campsites and plentiful freshwater in this heather-and-talus basin below Seven Fingered Jack; the standard overnight base for the Fernow/7FJ traverse.

waypoints.name: Notch on Seven Fingered Jack Ridge
waypoints.note: Climbers' path works up heather benches from Leroy Basin to this ridge notch, then drops toward Gloomy Basin to begin the traverse onto Fernow's southeast side.

waypoints.name: Gloomy Basin / Gloomy Glacier Moraine
waypoints.note: Roughly 1,000 ft of elevation is lost descending off the notch to cross the Gloomy Glacier's loose rocky moraine — a costly re-climb on the return leg for car-to-car parties.

waypoints.name: Loose talus/scree slopes below the southeast face
waypoints.note: Reported as some of the route's worst loose talus and scree; favor the narrow band of solid rock slabs near the snowmelt seeps for firmer footing.

waypoints.name: Mount Fernow Summit
waypoints.note: Exposed, loose class 4-5 summit block — roughly 200 ft of scrambling through a narrow notch ('cannonhole') to the true summit; down-climb this section with care on the descent.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead
waypoints.note: SR 20 milepost 134 parking lot; Northwest Forest Pass required. Descend the Ross Dam Trail toward the lake to reach Ross Lake Resort and arrange a paid water-taxi pickup.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 to the parking lot at milepost 134, roughly 28 miles east of Marblemount. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to leave a car here.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Landing (water-taxi drop)
waypoints.note: Ross Lake Resort's boat drops climbers here to skip miles of lakeshore trail; self-issue wilderness permit kiosk and start of the Big Beaver Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: Walk down the Ross Dam Trail toward the lake and arrange a paid water-taxi pickup with Ross Lake Resort; the boat runs seasonally, costs about $35 one way, and drops climbers at Big Beaver Landing. Parties who cannot get a boat hike roughly 6 miles of lakeshore trail up the west side of Ross Lake instead.

waypoints.name: Luna Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp on the maintained Big Beaver Creek Trail through old-growth forest, roughly 8 trail miles above Big Beaver Landing.
waypoints.directions: Self-issue a wilderness permit at the kiosk, then follow the maintained Big Beaver Creek Trail up-valley through old-growth cedar. It is about 8 to 10 trail miles of easy walking, passing the Big Beaver backcountry camp, to reach Luna Camp.

waypoints.name: Access Creek crossing
waypoints.note: About 1.5 miles past Luna Camp, leave the maintained trail and ford Big Beaver Creek to pick up the faint, cairned Access Creek climbers' path.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the maintained trail about another 1.5 miles past Luna Camp, then leave it and ford Big Beaver Creek to pick up the faint, cairned climbers' path up Access Creek. This is the single easiest place on the trip to go wrong: in poor visibility parties have committed to the wrong drainage, so find the cairns marking the correct crossing before you commit.

waypoints.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
waypoints.note: Cairned climbers' path up the north flank crosses to the creek's south bank near 3,700 ft where brush thickens, then continues to good camping at the basin below the Luna-McMillan col.
waypoints.directions: Climb steep, pathless forest and heather along the north flank of Access Creek. The cairned path crosses to the south bank near 3,700 ft where the brush thickens, then continues to break out of the timber into the open, meadow-floored basin below Luna Peak, which is far less brushy than the drainages either side of it. Reports call it a few hours of reasonable but sustained hiking.

waypoints.name: Luna Col
waypoints.note: Notch between Luna Peak and a small tower on the Luna-McMillan arm; a small snowfield at the saddle usually provides running water and there's a good camp spot here or ~150 ft below on the east side.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-basin past the camping area at the headwaters, then climb a steep gully and heather system to the notch near 6,100 ft that first opens the view north into Luna Cirque. From there a long sidehill traverse of steep heather and talus works around Luna Peak toward Luna Pass, with one short genuinely steep section and cliff-band route-finding, before gaining the connecting ridge to the col. A small snowfield on the saddle usually gives running water.

waypoints.name: East Fury (ridge traverse start)
waypoints.note: Higher of Fury's twin summits and the start of the ~5.4 YDS, Grade III ridge traverse over three towers to West Fury; loose, exposed rock — rope up for the gendarmes.
