waypoints.directions: Leave the col early on a light rack. Cross over Point 7360 and drop a red ledge system to a low-fifth-class crux tower, then climb the East Fury Glacier and arete to the summit. Most parties reach it around four to five hours out of camp.

waypoints.name: West Fury (Mount Fury, West Peak)
waypoints.note: True, officially-named summit of Mount Fury. Descend by reversing the ridge traverse to East Fury, then drop East Fury's east-side glacier/scree gully back to Luna Col.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the ridge over three loose towers, with short downclimbs and rappels connecting them. It is roughly 5.4 at its hardest, wildly exposed, and the rock is notoriously mobile choss rather than anything solid, so rope up for the gendarmes and expect two to three hours. Anchors are natural horns and slings you leave behind.

waypoints.name: Lake Serene Trailhead
waypoints.note: Off Mount Index Road (FSR 6020) then FSR 6020-109 near US 2 MP 35; Northwest Forest Pass required at the self-issue kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Leave US 2 near milepost 35 onto Mount Index Road (FSR 6020), then FSR 6020-109, and follow it to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and there is a self-issue kiosk at the trailhead if you do not already have one. Trail #1068 starts here and runs 4.1 miles up to the lake.

waypoints.name: Bridal Veil Falls creek crossing
waypoints.note: Spur trail climbs steep stairs to the falls viewpoint; the creek here can sweep hikers off their feet in high flow, so stay well back from the edge.

waypoints.name: North end of Lake Serene
waypoints.note: Maintained Trail No. 1068 ends at the lake beneath Mount Index's 3,000-ft cliff face; last reliable water before the climbers' path.

waypoints.name: Climbers' path / talus entry
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here on a rough boot path through talus toward the NE spur; the classic talus/rockslide entry is sometimes placed on the lake's opposite (west) shore, so expect route-finding uncertainty on either side.

waypoints.name: NE Spur gain point
waypoints.note: Scramble several hundred feet up the brushy NE spur to the first slab, staying just right of the crest per the North Face route description.

waypoints.name: North Face brush gullies / exposed corner pitch
waypoints.note: Wet, mossy slabs and a sharply exposed corner pitch above roughly 1,000 ft of air over Lake Serene; these are the same rope-eating, brushy gullies used on the rappel descent, so mark the line on the way up.

waypoints.name: Mount Index summit
waypoints.note: True summit at 5,991 ft; register/topout reached via the Class 5.0-5.6 North Face terrain above the spur.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead off Hwy 20; accesses Easy Pass/Fisher Creek Trail to Douglas Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: Drive Highway 20, the North Cascades Highway, to the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, at about 3,700 feet. Highway 20 is a seasonal route, typically open from mid-April through mid-November and closed the rest of the year, so check conditions before you go.

waypoints.name: Phelps Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-6211 (Phelps Creek Road), near Trinity, WA, Chelan County — the standard approach, replacing the previous (rare-alternate) Cottonwood Campground/Entiat River Road waypoint.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Chiwawa River Road (FR 62) roughly twenty-four miles, then turn onto the Phelps Creek Road, FR 6211, and follow it to its end at the Phelps Creek Trailhead (about 3,500 ft), near Trinity in Chelan County.

waypoints.name: Leroy Creek Crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Leroy Creek and leave the maintained Phelps Creek Trail for the unmaintained climbers' path north into Leroy Basin; coordinates shared with the sibling Seven Fingered Jack record for this same trail segment.

waypoints.name: Leroy Basin
waypoints.note: Standard base camp shared by Mount Maude, Seven Fingered Jack, and Mount Fernow climbs; coordinates shared with the sibling Seven Fingered Jack record.

waypoints.name: Mount Maude Summit
waypoints.note: True summit, reached from Leroy Basin via a ~7,700 ft col between Seven Fingered Jack and Maude, then the North Face (long, cornice-threatened snow/ice, best climbed before mid-July).

waypoints.name: Upper South Fork Skokomish Trailhead (Trail #873)
waypoints.note: Reached via Skokomish Valley Rd / FS-23 / FS-2361 from Shelton; FS-2361 gated Oct 1-Apr 30. Standard route follows Trail 873 to Sundown Lake, then the Six Ridge crest ~11 miles to the overgrown 'Mount Olson Way' spur.

waypoints.name: South Fork Skokomish River ford
waypoints.note: Unbridged ford of the Skokomish's south bank; safely crossable (ankle-deep) only in late summer/early fall low water, otherwise a serious hazard.

waypoints.name: Olympic National Park boundary
waypoints.note: Trail leaves Olympic National Forest and enters Olympic National Park/Wilderness; self-issue backcountry camping permit required beyond this point, tread grows fainter above here.

waypoints.name: Sundown Pass
waypoints.note: Forested saddle marked by a broken signpost, reached via steep, faint tread through wet subalpine meadows; junction with the Six Ridge Trail heading east along the crest toward Mount Olson.

waypoints.name: Lake Sundown
waypoints.note: Short spur off the pass to a subalpine basin lake on Six Ridge's western flank; last dependable water and the standard base camp for an Olson attempt.

waypoints.name: Six Ridge crest / Mount Olson boot-path junction
waypoints.note: Point on Six Ridge's sawtooth crest closest to Olson where an unsigned, unofficial boot path ('Mount Olson Way') leaves the trail for the peak; faint and overgrown with blowdowns and lingering snowfields into midsummer.

waypoints.name: Tarn below Olson's summit block
waypoints.note: Boulder-field tarn just below the summit block is the last water and a common bivy spot; the final gully above it to the top is steep, loose, and exposed.

waypoints.name: White River Campground
waypoints.note: Approach via Glacier Basin and St. Elmo Pass.

waypoints.name: Nooksack Cirque Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 34 (via Mt Baker Hwy SR 542, Hannegan Pass Rd FR 32, then FR 34); ford Ruth Creek immediately at the trailhead — no bridge, wade it or cross a downed log if present.
waypoints.directions: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 12.5 miles, then turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32). Continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR-34) and follow FR-34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead, which is a different trailhead from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR-32. Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there's no bridge, so wade it or cross a downed log if one is present, and note that early-summer high water can make the crossing difficult or unsafe.

waypoints.name: Leave Trail #750 roadbed
waypoints.note: About 50 minutes up the old logging roadbed (Trail #750), leave the trail and begin an ascending traverse up through forest toward Sefrit's west/southwest ridge — no path, route-finding required.

waypoints.name: Brushy ascending traverse
waypoints.note: Steep forest with slide alder and old avalanche debris on the traverse toward the ridge crest — slick brush and rotten downed timber slow travel on this south-facing approach.

waypoints.name: 5800' meadows on ridge crest
waypoints.note: Brush opens into subalpine meadows around 5800 ft on the ridge, giving easy open travel across to the summit gully — the same feature noted in trip reports of the parallel south-side route off this trailhead.

waypoints.name: Class 4 summit gully
waypoints.note: Loose, blocky Class 4 gully breaches the final rock band to the summit ridge; this is the gully down-climbed on the reverse descent per the on-file beta.

waypoints.name: Mount Sefrit summit
waypoints.note: Broad rocky summit block 4 miles north of Mount Shuksan, overlooking the Nooksack Cirque and North Fork Nooksack headwaters.

waypoints.name: Whiskey Bend Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of the Elwha River Trail; Olympic Hot Springs Road is washed out beyond Madison Falls, adding roughly 6.9 mi of walking or biking each way just to reach this trailhead.

waypoints.name: Mary's Falls Camp
waypoints.note: Established riverside camp with reliable water from the Elwha River, roughly the halfway point to Hayes River.

waypoints.name: Hayes River Guard Station
waypoints.note: Historic patrol cabin and backcountry camp beside the Elwha River; the maintained trail continues upvalley toward Chicago Camp and Low Divide from here.

waypoints.name: Camp Wilder
waypoints.note: Backcountry camp (tent sites, bear wire, shelter) about 3.7 mi past Hayes River; leave the maintained trail here per route beta and head cross-country toward the upper Elwha Basin.

waypoints.name: Upper Elwha Basin
waypoints.note: Open heather benches and headwater creeks below Mount Wilder's south face; the last reliable water before the scree/talus climb to the ridge.

waypoints.name: South-Face Scree/Talus Slope
waypoints.note: Loose scree and talus on a slope that gains nearly 3,800 ft in under 2 miles on this south aspect; watch for rockfall and keep the party close together.

waypoints.name: Mount Wilder Summit
waypoints.note: True summit via the Class 2 south ridge; the southernmost peak of the Bailey Range, with Mount Olympus visible 8.7 mi WNW.

waypoints.name: Stafford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 9703; ~20-car lot with pit toilet, Northwest Forest Pass or $5 self-issue fee required; trail has seen closures for Labor Mountain Fire damage so check current USFS alerts before going.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Teanaway River Road to 29 Pines Campground, bear right where the pavement ends, then turn onto Stafford Creek Road and follow it a couple of miles to where it ends at the trailhead. The last stretch is dirt and washboarded but passable to low-clearance cars in dry conditions.

waypoints.name: Stafford Creek crossing, Stafford Creek Meadows
waypoints.note: Stream crossing in the meadows on Trail #1359; last reliable water before the drier climb toward the pass.
waypoints.directions: Trail #1359 leaves the lot at an easy grade through dry ponderosa and lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek most of the way. A short rerouted section of steeper switchbacks near the half-mile mark bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread. The forest stays open and the grade never gets hard before the trail reaches the marshy meadow ground.

waypoints.name: Standup Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail #1359 meets the Standup Creek Trail about 1 mile below Navaho Pass; continue straight/left on #1359 toward the pass.
waypoints.directions: Stay on Stafford Creek Trail #1359, still gaining gradually along the creek, to the signed junction with the Standup Creek Trail (#1369).

waypoints.name: Upper meadow camp
waypoints.note: Established camp area in the upper meadow (elev/dist interpolated between the 4,800 ft creek crossing and the pass); common overnight staging spot before the steep push above.
waypoints.directions: Continue on Trail #1359 above the junction; the trail opens out into a large, marshy subalpine meadow with a feeder stream — another water source, and the usual base camp for parties splitting the trip over two days.

waypoints.name: Navaho Pass
waypoints.note: Junction with the old County Line Trail (Cascade Creek Trail #1217); barren, rocky 'moon-scape' terrain with big Enchantments views, but very exposed to wind for camping.
waypoints.directions: Above the meadow the trail leaves the trees and switchbacks up open, rocky slope for the last stretch, gaining roughly 500 ft to the saddle. There is no water and essentially no shade on this section, and on the dry east side it bakes on a warm afternoon.

waypoints.name: South ridge scramble path
waypoints.note: Steep climber's path of loose scree and dirt gaining the south ridge; snow patches can linger into July, making poles/microspikes worthwhile.
waypoints.directions: From the pass turn east and follow the crest trail a short way toward the peak, then leave it where a boot path breaks off uphill onto the south ridge. The path is loose scree over dirt and steepens quickly, so poles earn their keep and it is easy to push rock down onto anyone below you.

waypoints.name: Navaho Peak
waypoints.note: True summit at 7,223 ft on the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary; panoramic views of the Enchantments and Stuart Range.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest up for a bit over 600 ft of gain on broken rock and scree; the scrambling stays easy Class 2 with hands wanted only occasionally. Stay on the ridge line rather than dropping onto the looser slopes on either side, which are steeper than they look from above.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: North end of the main Alpental Ski Area parking lot, off Alpental Rd near Snoqualmie Pass (I-90 exit 52); standard approach for New York Gully via Snow Lake trail then Phantom Slide/Source Lake basin.

waypoints.name: Snoqualmie Mountain summit
waypoints.note: This route is on Snoqualmie Mountain's NW face, not Chair Peak, reached from the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead.

waypoints.name: Nooksack Cirque Trailhead (Trail #750)
waypoints.note: Same road-end trailhead as the East Ridge route. The first-ascent party camped on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque area, then downclimbed/rappelled to the East Nooksack Glacier to reach the base of the South Face — i.e. the same Nooksack Cirque valley approach, just continuing further around/over to the back (south) side of the peak rather than staying on the ridge.

waypoints.name: Cedar Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: USFS Trail #476 trailhead off SR-20 near milepost 175-176, west of Winthrop.

waypoints.name: Slate Pass / Buckskin Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) near Slate Peak; self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk, road typically open only July-Sept.
waypoints.directions: Drive Forest Road 5400 from Mazama up to Harts Pass, published at roughly 6,181-6,204 feet - trailers are prohibited past the 5400000/5400060 junction because the road is narrow and steep with few turnouts, and whether an ordinary car should attempt it is genuinely disputed, so judge it on the day. At the guard station turn right onto FR 5400-600; the Pacific Crest Trail trailhead is at the first switchback and Slate Pass, at about 6,900 feet, is at the second. Early in the season you may have to walk the last half mile or so if the road isn't yet clear, and the road itself typically doesn't open until early-to-mid July depending on snowpack. Self-issue a Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk here.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten (Robinson Creek) Trail junction
waypoints.note: Reached via Buckskin Ridge Trail (0.9 mi) then Whistler Cutoff Trail (3.1 mi), dropping ~1,900 ft off the pass before turning south down the Middle Fork Pasayten drainage.
waypoints.directions: This leg is all downhill: drop off the pass on the Buckskin Ridge tread, then swing onto the Whistler Cutoff for a well-graded cruise to the valley floor. The first pitch below the pass holds snow well into summer and some parties carry an axe for it. The Middle Fork is crossed unbridged, usually ankle to shin deep in normal summer flow, but it deserves respect during snowmelt or after heavy rain.

waypoints.name: Eureka Creek Trail (#484) junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail here and start climbing east up Eureka Creek toward Freds Lake; the way tread is brushy and blowdown-choked beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: Turn south and follow the Middle Fork Pasayten trail up the valley. Tread through here is generally good and brush-free, and it is the fastest walking of the trip. Watch for the signed turnoff, which is easy to stride past when the miles are going quickly.

waypoints.name: Freds Lake
waypoints.note: Larch-ringed lake with reliable water and informal camping, the usual overnight stop before pushing on to Freds Pass.
waypoints.directions: Climb east up the Eureka Creek drainage. This is where the trip changes character: tread narrows, brush closes in and stepping over blowdown becomes routine, so expect the pace to drop noticeably. The grade is steady rather than steep, gaining roughly 1,200 ft to the lake basin.

waypoints.name: Freds Pass
waypoints.note: Trail contours Freds Lake's north shore then climbs the head of the basin to this saddle, the gateway into the upper Eureka Creek / Lake Doris basin.
waypoints.directions: Roughly 600 ft of climbing packed into half a mile, which makes this the steepest sustained trail section of the approach. The saddle is open and exposed with no water on it, so top off at the lake before starting up.

waypoints.name: Lake Doris
waypoints.note: Alpine lake basin serving as the standard base camp for Osceola's west slopes; the scramble route starts on the ridge north of the lake.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and contour down into the next basin, only a couple of hundred feet of loss over about half a mile. Snow can linger on this side early in the season. This is the last water and the standard camp, and everything above it is dry.

waypoints.name: Southwest talus/slab slope
waypoints.note: Loose, sharp talus mixed with slabs that get slick with wet lichen; trip reports describe staying on faint use-trail through the least-bad line rather than the slabs.
waypoints.directions: From the lake head northeast through open forest and onto the slope above, aiming for the southwest ridge rather than straight up the south-face boulder field. There is a faint use trail on the ridge and it is far better going than the slabs, which turn genuinely slick where lichen is wet. Figure about 800 ft of gain to reach this point.

waypoints.name: Osceola Peak
waypoints.note: True summit (8,587 ft); broad talus top with views to Mount Lago and Carru across upper Eureka Creek.
waypoints.directions: Continue up on big talus broken by short sections of scree, staying on the faint trail wherever it shows rather than drifting onto the slabs. It is Class 2 with occasional Class 3 steps and about another 800 ft of gain to the broad summit. Nothing here needs a rope, and the descent reverses the same line.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Unpaved pullout off Goodell Creek Rd, just before Goodell Creek Campground, across SR-20 from Newhalem; standard access for all Southern Pickets objectives via the Terror Creek climbers' trail.
waypoints.directions: Take the gravel road that forks off Highway 20 across from Newhalem and follow it to where it dead-ends at a gravel pit, at about 600 feet — there is parking here but no trailhead sign. The unpaved pullout sits just before Goodell Creek Campground and is the standard access point for Southern Pickets objectives via the Terror Creek climbers' path. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required.

waypoints.name: Large cairn off the old roadbed
waypoints.note: Cairn/arrow marks where the climbers' path leaves the Goodell Creek roadbed toward Terror Creek and Crescent Creek Basin.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek ford
waypoints.note: Ford on foot near a cairn on the far bank; typically no more than calf-deep by midsummer but can run high and cold earlier in the season.

waypoints.name: Forested ridge crest, toe of the Barrier
waypoints.note: Steep climbers' path tops out on the ridge between Terror and Crescent Creeks here; this is the base of 'the Barrier' rock rib you cross next.

waypoints.name: The Barrier crossing
waypoints.note: Loose, dirty Class 3 traverse with exposed moves crossing the Barrier's rock rib into the Terror/Crescent Creek basins; rockfall risk on the loose sections.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Established basin camp used for Ottohorn, Himmelhorn, and the Chopping Block; reached after crossing the Barrier.

waypoints.name: Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
waypoints.note: About an hour above camp with some dicey scrambling near the top; gain the col here then follow the 1961 line onto Ottohorn's east ridge (Class III). South side of the col is the easier descent, the north side turns to loose low-5th once melted out.

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard access point via FR-56/Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road; no day-use fee is currently charged at this specific trailhead (per USFS), though a free self-issue wilderness permit is required beyond it for Alpine Lakes Wilderness travel, and the road washout beyond this point means biking or hiking the closed roadbed toward Dutch Miller Gap.
waypoints.directions: FR-56 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to the lot is heavily potholed and rutted; parties in low-clearance cars routinely park short and walk the last stretch, which adds to an already long day.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Lake
waypoints.note: Standard high camp for the route, roughly 10 mi in via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail/old roadbed then a steep, unmaintained forested slog above a river ford near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trail; seldom-visited alpine lake below the Overcoat Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: The continuation of the road past the gate is roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed to Hardscrabble Horse Camp, and most parties bike it rather than walk it. Beyond that the Dutch Miller Gap Trail runs east along the north bank; the tread is reasonable but summer thimbleberry buries the rocks underfoot. Leave the trail about a mile before it swings toward Williams Lake and ford the river: it can run thigh-to-waist deep, and it is colder and higher on the way back than it was in the morning.

waypoints.name: Rock benches above Overcoat Glacier
waypoints.note: Higher alternate camp on open benches used to shorten summit day; on-file route beta cites roughly 6,600 ft for this bivy option.
waypoints.directions: Above the ford the ground climbs steeply through brush into a rocky corridor of waterfalls and steep faces before opening onto snow and benches. Snow lingers here well past midsummer. The awkward part is a sloping rock step partway up, which is markedly harder to downclimb than to climb and is worth noting for the return.

waypoints.name: Notch on Overcoat Peak's north ridge (Overcoat Col)
waypoints.note: Contour east from camp to this notch to gain the upper Overcoat Glacier; a col of the same name and elevation (~6,800 ft) sits beneath Chimney Rock's east face.
waypoints.directions: Only a couple of hundred feet of net gain, but it is a rising traverse over benches and old snow rather than a walk. The glacier starts immediately on the far side, so rope up and fit crampons at the notch rather than after stepping onto it.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the glacier's lower snowfields toward the peak's southeast side; local trip reports warn of deep crevasses and weak, undermined snow bridges on this rapidly retreating glacier.
waypoints.directions: Drop onto the upper glacier from the notch and work toward the peak's southeast side. Most parties time this route for the tail end of summer, when the crevasses are open and visible and the rock above is clear of snow; earlier in the season the bridges are the thing that will catch you out.

waypoints.name: Snow finger to east face
waypoints.note: Find the snow finger leading off the glacier onto the east face here, then pick up the Class 3-4 ledges and heathery gully toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: The finger rises off the top of the glacier and is steep enough that crampons and a second tool are the norm. A crevasse commonly cuts it partway up and has to be turned. Near the dark towers at its top, move off snow onto rock and round the corner east to reach the ledge system.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; the final ~400 vertical ft is a Class 4/low-5.0 heathery gully leading to an angled chimney, per climbers' trip reports, with a small summit register.
waypoints.directions: The gully has solid holds but a few tall steps force committing, exposed moves, and most parties pitch it out on small cams and nuts in mediocre rock rather than soloing it. Sort the descent before you commit: the damp dihedral below is normally rappelled twice, not downclimbed.

waypoints.name: Reflection Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: South side of Stevens Canyon Road at the Reflection Lakes parking pullouts; Mount Rainier NP entrance fee applies, no water at the lot.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road, at about 4,860 ft. It is a small paved pullout lot and it fills early on weekends, so plan an early arrival. A Mount Rainier National Park entrance fee applies, and there is no water at the lot, so fill up before you get here. The trail is signed but unnumbered and starts directly across Stevens Canyon Road from the parking. When the road is snow-gated, winter parties start instead from the Narada Falls pullout.

waypoints.name: Seasonal Stream Crossing
waypoints.note: Small seasonal stream crosses the trail; often dry by late summer so don't rely on it for resupply.

waypoints.name: Cliff Bands Below Trail
waypoints.note: Trail runs directly beneath exposed cliff bands here; watch for rockfall and loose debris, especially if goats or other hikers are above.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Saddle
waypoints.note: Maintained NPS trail ends at this 5,920-ft saddle between Pinnacle and Plummer Peaks; unmarked climber's path to the summit gully begins on the south side.

waypoints.name: Base of Summit Gully
waypoints.note: Climber's path traverses goat trails and loose scree around the peak's south side to reach the start of the class 3-4 ascent gully.

waypoints.name: Summit Gully Scramble
waypoints.note: NPS warns this is a precipitous scramble on loose, unstable rock; trip reports cite a few class 3 moves with real exposure, so avoid climbing directly below other parties.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit and second-highest point in the Tatoosh Range, with sweeping views of Rainier, Adams, and St. Helens.

waypoints.name: Reflection Lakes / Pinnacle Peak Trailhead
waypoints.note: ~35-car unpaved pullout on the south side of Stevens Canyon Road, directly across from Reflection Lakes; trail sign for Pinnacle Peak/Plummer Peak starts here.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road, about 1.4 miles east of the Paradise-Longmire Road junction and roughly 1.9 miles from the Paradise turnoff — an unpaved pullout on the south side of the road with room for about 35 cars, directly across from the largest of the Reflection Lakes. The signed trail for Pinnacle Peak/Plummer Peak starts right there; it's a maintained Mount Rainier National Park trail with no official number. Stevens Canyon Road is open roughly late May through late October, and this small lot commonly fills by mid-morning on summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Seasonal stream crossing
waypoints.note: A small seasonal stream crosses the switchbacks partway up; flows well early season but can run dry by late July-August.

waypoints.name: Cliff-band switchbacks below the saddle
waypoints.note: Trail steepens onto loose rock with exposed drop-offs on the final switchbacks before the saddle; NPS specifically warns of unstable rock and steep edges here, worse with lingering snow.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Saddle
waypoints.note: T-intersection between Pinnacle and Plummer Peaks where the maintained trail ends; climber's boot path continues right/east to Pinnacle, left/west toward Plummer.

waypoints.name: Heather-and-talus boot path to Plummer's summit block
waypoints.note: Unmaintained Class 2 boot path across heather and loose talus with sparse cairns; easy to lose the path in cloud or on the descent.

waypoints.name: Plummer Peak summit
waypoints.note: Broad rocky summit (7th-highest in the Tatoosh Range) with views north to Rainier and south to Adams, St. Helens, and Hood on clear days.

waypoints.name: Westside Road / Dry Creek (Tahoma Creek) Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of driveable Westside Road (3.2 mi from the Nisqually-Longmire Rd junction), gated at Dry Creek. CHECK THIS BEFORE YOU DRIVE: the National Park Service's own page for Indian Henry's Hunting Ground — the next waypoint on this route — lists only two accesses to it, Kautz Creek (11.5 mi round trip) and Longmire (13 mi round trip). The Westside Road and Tahoma Creek corridor is not among them, and route beta for Success Cleaver reports the Tahoma Creek Trail closed for flood hazard, leaving Longmire via the Wonderland Trail as the standard approach. The mileages recorded on this route's waypoints are measured from this Dry Creek gate, so they describe the older corridor rather than a Longmire or Kautz Creek start — treat them as approximate if you approach from either of those, and confirm current trail status with a wilderness information centre.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 706 to the Nisqually Entrance in the park's south-west corner; the road is paved and open essentially year round, conditions permitting. Westside Road leaves the Nisqually to Longmire road and is driveable about three miles to the gate at Dry Creek, where a standing, non-seasonal closure caused by repeated Tahoma Creek washouts stops vehicles; past the gate it is open to foot and bike traffic only. Longmire, where the nearest wilderness information centre is and where you register in and out, lies about 3.5 miles further along the main road.

waypoints.name: Indian Henry's Hunting Ground (patrol cabin)
waypoints.note: Historic 1915 patrol cabin marks where the route leaves the maintained Wonderland Trail for cross-country travel toward the Mirror Lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Mirror Lakes
waypoints.note: Small tarns about a mile off the Wonderland Trail; last dependable water before contouring dry southwest/west slopes of Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained Wonderland Trail at the patrol cabin and take the Mirror Lakes spur west, crossing marshy meadow on a series of plank walkways. Maintained tread ends part way along and the path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft, in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak, roughly a mile off the Wonderland. These tarns are the last dependable water before the dry south-west and west slopes of Pyramid Peak.

waypoints.name: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
waypoints.note: Flat campsites just north of this 6,631 ft high point give broad views of Success Cleaver; no sourced GPS fix found, position estimated from route beta contouring Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: From the tarns it is cross-country travel. Head north-east out of the basin and contour the south-west then west slopes of Pyramid Peak, staying roughly between 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. There is no boot-pack and only sparse cairning through here, so carry a map or GPS track and expect to find your own line; snowmelt water is often available around the point into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak near 6,300 ft is a common first night.

waypoints.name: 6,400 ft saddle below Success Cleaver
waypoints.note: Short descent NNE from Point 6631 to this saddle; typical high camp before scrambling onto the lower cleaver at first light.
waypoints.directions: Drop north-north-east from Point 6631 a short way to the saddle at about 6,400 ft, which is the start of Success Cleaver proper. It is a scree and loose-boulder col and it looks unpleasant, which is how you know it is the right place. There is an easier way down into it than the obvious line, and parties record missing it and taking the worst ground, so pick the descent out before you commit and note it for the return.

waypoints.name: Lower Success Cleaver gendarmes
waypoints.note: Loose rock towers force weaving route-finding on the lower rib; rockfall risk climbs if other parties are above; bivy options around 8,100-8,300 ft.
waypoints.directions: From the col the cleaver rises straight ahead and does not let up: loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, no track and no cairned line, weaving among rock towers on ground you route-find yourself. Use what is on either side as the test. The South Tahoma Glacier should fall away to climber's left and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to climber's right; if you find yourself on a glacier, or if the going out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you have drifted off the cleaver and are contouring around Pyramid Peak instead. Rockfall risk rises sharply with any party above you, the rock firms up above roughly 7,000 ft, and there are bivy sites around 8,100 to 8,300 ft.

waypoints.name: Rockfall chutes to Kautz Cleaver headwall
waypoints.note: Angle across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall and gain the Kautz Cleaver near 12,600 ft; helmet mandatory, best crossed before sun loosens rock.
waypoints.directions: Follow the cleaver crest up through class 3 and short class 4 rock bands and steep chutes, past bivy benches near 9,400 ft and the small col at about 10,700 ft. Higher, the crest holds a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow has melted off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies and across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall, joining the Kautz Cleaver between roughly 12,200 and 12,600 ft. Cross those chutes early, before the sun starts releasing rock and ice; helmets on.

waypoints.name: Point Success
waypoints.directions: From the Kautz Cleaver climb steepening snow and ice, generally around 45 degrees, to the headwall below the summit. A cliff band bars the way and is passed either by a short low fifth class rock step, exposed and sometimes wet or icy, or by an isolated snow and ice pitch of about 15 ft at up to 55 degrees, depending on the season. Above it the angle eases onto the summit plateau at Point Success, 14,158 ft.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Mine Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Sunrise Mine Road (NF-4065), 2.3 mi off Mountain Loop Highway; Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Headlee Pass
waypoints.note: Steep, loose switchbacks up the old mining trail top out at this notch between Sperry and Morning Star Peaks; can hold snow into July.

waypoints.name: Vesper Lake (Lake Elan)
waypoints.note: Filter water at the lake outlet before continuing up-basin; last reliable water before the climb.

waypoints.name: Saddle/col between Vesper and Wolf Peak (cairned pass)
Ragged Edge route start (north face ledge)
Vesper Peak Summit
waypoints.note: P6, the signature 'ragged edge' arete pitch, tops out on the true summit; descend the East Ridge back to the Vesper-Sperry saddle and out via Headlee Pass.

waypoints.name: Wine Spires / Silver Star Trailhead (SR-20 MP 166)
waypoints.note: Pullout ~4mi east of Washington Pass, signed for Silver Star Mountain, serving the whole Wine Spires cluster including Paisano Pinnacle.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the pullout near milepost 166, roughly 4 miles east of Washington Pass at about 4,300 feet. This is the Wine Spires parking and it serves the whole cluster, Paisano Pinnacle included. Park on the shoulder — the boot path drops straight off the pullout down talus toward Early Winters Creek, so no further driving is needed.

waypoints.name: Bench Camp spring
waypoints.note: Fresh water at the Larch/Bench Camp below the Wine Spires cirque; reached via steep climbers trail from the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166.

waypoints.name: Paisano Pinnacle - Summit
waypoints.note: Rampage route to the summit.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required; parking lot is just past the Downey Creek bridge on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), about 20 mi from Hwy 530.
waypoints.directions: Drive Suiattle River Road (FR 26) about 20 miles in from Highway 530; the parking area sits just past the Downey Creek bridge at roughly 1,450 feet. Display a Northwest Forest Pass. Check the road before you commit to the trip, because it is frequently washed out or gated well short of the trailhead, adding miles of walking or biking each way that none of the trail mileage here accounts for. The route is normally in condition July through September.

waypoints.name: Sixmile Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp along the easy, flat Downey Creek Trail #768 where the route leaves the maintained trail and turns east along Bachelor Creek.
waypoints.directions: Follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles from the trailhead — easy, well-graded and mostly flat through forest, with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford or log-cross Bachelor Creek to its south side here; the climbers' path above is badly overgrown with slide alder up to roughly 4,400 ft.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends here; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first, then ford to the south side at about the 9.5-mile mark. Treat it as a real creek crossing — harder and more dangerous in high water or early season.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake Pass
waypoints.note: Gap on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake (~5,880 ft), gained by switchbacks; begin the ~500 ft descent to the lake basin from here.
waypoints.directions: Climb the climbers' path above the crossing. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone, so expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber; above the debris the path climbs to the pass on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake
waypoints.note: High camp with reliable water at the lake basin; Itswoot Ridge, reached by traversing further, is the alternate camp some parties use instead.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 500 ft off the pass into the lake basin. These are snow slopes into midsummer and this is normally the crux navigation of the approach day when they are covered.

waypoints.name: Dome Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the Dome Glacier's crevasses toward the Dome-Sinister col; trip reports describe a bergschrund spanning the glacier that requires finding a solid snowbridge.
waypoints.directions: Most parties push on from the lake basin up onto Itswoot Ridge for high camp, then traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the glacier. Rope up for glacier travel and carry crevasse-rescue gear before starting across.

waypoints.name: Dome-Sinister col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Dome and Sinister Peaks; from here contour on an easy snowfield around to Sinister's south side to reach the loose southwest gully.
waypoints.directions: Cross over the Dome–Chikamin col and descend the crevassed Chikamin Glacier to about 7,200 ft, then traverse right (east) across the glacier to the col. The bergschrund guarding it can be hard to cross in late season and has sometimes required a short rappel to get down onto or across it.

waypoints.name: Sinister Peak
waypoints.note: True summit, just under a mile east of Dome Peak along the connecting ridge; reached via the loose southwest gully to the upper west ridge.
waypoints.directions: From the col contour around on an easy snowfield to Sinister's south side, then climb the loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge and scramble Class 2–3 along the ridge to the top. Loose rock in the gully is the main hazard — move fast and keep the party out of each other's fall line; some parties skip it and take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col.

waypoints.name: Surprise Lake
waypoints.note: Trail switchbacks above the lake to join the PCT. Coordinate and elevation corrected to the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife's published position for Surprise Lake (King County); the Forest Service's Surprise Creek Trail #1060 page independently gives the lake at 4,500 ft. The previous pin sat 5.2 mi west, which is the same ~4.5 mi westward error this route's other waypoints were already corrected for.

waypoints.name: Trap Pass
waypoints.note: PCT junction; the climbers path to Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower leaves directly from the top of the pass.

waypoints.name: Base of Slippery Slab Tower
waypoints.note: Corrected — an earlier coordinate (47.665,-121.22) sat ~4.5mi west of Trap Pass instead of continuing toward the tower, likely a data entry error. This pin (47.668645,-121.126119, elev 6356ft) matches the area's own registered location.

waypoints.name: Slippery Slab Tower NE Face Topout
waypoints.note: Corrected — an earlier coordinate (47.6636,-121.2226) was ~4.5mi off; this pin is cross-checked against the area's own registered location. Two-pitch 5.4; Pitch 2 diagonals left into a gully to a large boulder near the top.

waypoints.name: Tunnel Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: FS Rd 6095, ~13.2 mi east of Skykomish off US-2; approach is Tunnel Creek Trail -> PCT (Hope Lake) -> south to Trap Pass -> climbers trail to NE base of tower

waypoints.name: Snow Lakes
waypoints.note: Trail continues up past the lakes toward Enchantment Basin.

waypoints.name: Viviane Campsite (Lake Viviane)
waypoints.note: Reached after climbing ~6,400 vertical ft; limited campsites on either side of the lake outlet, adjacent to the crag.

waypoints.name: Base of Prusik Peak south face (approximate)
waypoints.note: Approximate — no reliable topout coordinate was found, so this reuses the Viviane Campsite coordinate; the climbing zone is right at the base of Prusik Peak's south face/west ridge near the camp.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (Trail #1599)
waypoints.note: From Snow Lakes TH, hike Snow Lakes Trail #1553 up through Nada Lake/Snow Lakes and the Enchantment basin to Lake Viviane, where the crag sits directly alongside the trail.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Corrected - previous waypoints incorrectly placed this route ~59 miles away at Amphitheater Mountain (Pasayten Wilderness), a research error. South Peak is actually part of the Gunsight Range, Glacier Peak Wilderness - same remote 2-day approach as Middle Peak (Downey/Bachelor Creek trail to Itswoot Ridge, Dome-Chickamin col, Chickamin Glacier).

waypoints.name: South Peak (Gunsight Range)
waypoints.note: A real, distinct summit — the southernmost of four named summits (Northeast/North/Middle/South) along one short ridge crest, reached last in a north-to-south traverse after Middle Peak. This coordinate is a disclosed geometric estimate ~0.2mi south of Middle Peak's position (48.30571,-120.99439) along the ridge, not a directly measured fix.

waypoints.name: Holden Village / Railroad Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Via ferry+bus to Holden Village, then Railroad Creek Trail ~3.5mi to Hart Lake (3,956ft), then off-trail up rock/heather terraces ~3,000ft to a camp near the 7,100ft pass between Bonanza and North Star Peak, then talus to the buttress base.
waypoints.directions: No road reaches this trailhead. Drive to Chelan or Field's Point Landing and take the Lady of the Lake ferry roughly four hours up the lake to Lucerne, then ride the Forest Service and Holden Village bus the remaining miles up to Holden Village at about 3,300 ft, where the Railroad Creek Trail begins. Check access before you commit to the ferry: FR 8301 between Lucerne and Holden, and Holden Village itself, closed after the December 2025 flood and landslide, under a Forest Service order running into 2027.

waypoints.name: Hart Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable, ice-cold water source and the last easy camp option before the route's steep terraces begin.
waypoints.directions: From Holden Village follow the Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) west up the valley about 3.5 miles to Hart Lake at 3,956 ft. Stay on the main valley trail the whole way; the Holden Lake Trail branches off partway along and is not your turn. The lake is the last easy water and the last straightforward camp before the off-trail ground starts.

waypoints.name: Rock and heather terraces
waypoints.note: Steep, loose rock-and-heather terraces gain most of the ~3,000 ft to high camp; exposed Class 3-4 scrambling in spots.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at Hart Lake and fill water, because the terraces above hold very little of it. Climb out of the lake basin onto the rock and heather terraces on the west side of the drainage, staying left of the waterfalls and cliff bands that come down off Bonanza's west-facing buttress. There is no path above the lake, and the lower slopes are brushy and loose with exposed Class 3 to 4 scrambling in places, so this leg is routefinding rather than trail walking.

waypoints.name: High camp near North Star-Bonanza pass (~7,100 ft)
waypoints.note: Flat, parklike camp with water available, about 2.5 hours above Hart Lake, just south of the pass between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak.
waypoints.directions: Keep working up the terrace system as open forest gives way to heather benches and then blocky, loose ground, roughly 3,000 ft of gain above Hart Lake taking most parties two and a half to three hours. Aim for the 7,100 ft pass between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak. Camp is the flat, parklike bench just south of the pass, with snowmelt water nearby, and it is the last water before the climb.

waypoints.name: Buttress base
waypoints.note: Under an hour across talus from camp to the start of the route, roughly 60 ft above the buttress's lowest point; first pitch is a narrow chimney.
waypoints.directions: From camp, cross the talus basin to the foot of the buttress, a little under an hour of walking on loose blocks with no trail. The climb starts at the toe of the buttress about 60 ft above its lowest point, where a narrow chimney takes the first pitch. Parties on a 5 AM start reach the base in time to begin climbing at first light.

waypoints.name: Crux pitches, middle third of buttress
waypoints.note: Three sustained pitches of 5.9-5.10a in the middle of the route, the technical crux above a horizontal bypass ledge and cave belay.
waypoints.directions: Climb the buttress from the toe: a narrow chimney, then broad licheny face climbing along the crest where blocks are worth testing before you weight them, a steepening face that prompts the change into rock shoes, and a thin 5.9. Around pitch 5 the line steps onto the left, east wall to skirt a headwall directly above, and pitch 6 finishes at a sheltered cave alcove that is the standard belay before the hard climbing. Above the cave, sustained chimneys and stemming lead into the three consecutive 5.9 to 5.10a pitches that form the technical crux.

waypoints.name: Bonanza Peak - Southwest Peak (estimated position)
waypoints.directions: Above the crux band, an easier pitch gains the sloping ramp that cuts diagonally across the buttress crest from east to west. That ramp is the key piece of routefinding on the climb, since it bypasses two headwalls that block a direct line. Follow it and the ledge system beyond onto a wildly exposed knife-edge connection to the upper tower, where the rock turns visibly redder and looser below a final overhanging headwall pitch topping out on the Southwest Peak at 9,320 ft.

waypoints.name: Northeast Ridge traverse to West Peak
waypoints.note: Exposed, gendarmed ridge traverse (~2 hr) from the Southwest Peak to the West Peak before dropping off the NW side via talus and two ~200-ft rappels.
waypoints.directions: From the Southwest Peak summit, the Northeast Ridge traverse toward the West Peak begins: about two hours of gendarmes turned mostly on 3rd and 4th class ledges with one short rappel.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start point for the 2-day approach (Hannegan Pass -> Easy Ridge -> Pickell Pass) used on this route's first ascent.
waypoints.directions: Drive Forest Road 32, the Hannegan Pass Road, to its end at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,120 ft. The road is normally open to the trailhead through summer and early fall but has a documented history of washout damage needing bypass construction, so confirm current status with the Glacier Public Service Center before driving in. Park with a Northwest Forest or interagency pass displayed; the overnight wilderness permit for everything past Hannegan Pass is a separate Park Service permit picked up in Glacier or Marblemount.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail (#674); stay on the maintained trail here and descend into the Chilliwack valley; the cross-country toward Easy Ridge starts far below, after the river ford, and the Copper Ridge trail branches down in the valley rather than at the pass.
waypoints.directions: Follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley, about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to the 5,050 ft pass, with Mount Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge across the valley. The grade is gentle and the tread is good the whole way, and the Ruth Creek crossings in the first couple of miles carry reliable water.

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River ford
waypoints.note: Ford the Chilliwack River below Easy Ridge on the climbers' path past Copper Creek before switchbacking back up; can be a cold, thigh-deep crossing in early season.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the maintained trail keeps going, and this is the stretch people get wrong: do not leave it here. Descend the switchbacks north-east into the Chilliwack valley, losing about 1,500 ft over roughly three miles to the Copper Creek area at a little over 3,000 ft, where the Copper Ridge trail branches away and is not your turn. Continue past it on the climbers' path and drop to the Chilliwack River ford below Easy Ridge. The crossing is cold and can run thigh-deep in early season, so pick a braided section, unclip your hipbelt, and cross before the afternoon melt comes down. The climbers' path switchbacks straight back up the far side, so this low point at 3,600 ft is the bottom of the whole approach.

waypoints.name: Bivy beyond Easy Peak
waypoints.note: Established climbers' bivy near the summit of Easy Peak (6,613'), reached via the Easy Ridge climbers' path gained above Hannegan Pass; typical end of day one.
waypoints.directions: From the river, switchback steeply back up onto Easy Ridge and then follow the crest itself. This is a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge with almost no shade; flowing water shows up relatively early along it, but the first-ascent party warned this stretch would be brutal later in the season and in dry years, so fill up while you can. Continue along and over Easy Peak to the established bivy beyond it, roughly a ten-hour day with a full pack from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Imperfect Impasse
waypoints.note: A notch on Easy Ridge that must be downclimbed and re-ascended to continue toward the Pickets proper; exposed and slower than it looks from a distance.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp and keep going along the ridge off-trail toward the Pickets, dropping to the cleft known as the Imperfect Impasse. This leg is route-finding and exposed scrambling rather than walking, and the notch has to be downclimbed and then re-ascended on the far side; parties consistently find it slower than it looks from a distance.

waypoints.name: Challenger Col
waypoints.note: Snow/glacier col that gains the western slope of the range; parties have noted a bergschrund forming near its top by mid-to-late season.
waypoints.directions: Out of the notch, regain elevation onto the flank of Mount Challenger and climb through Challenger Col. This is snow and glacier ground rather than rock, so rope up and treat it as crevassed terrain; parties have reported a bergschrund opening near the top of the col by mid to late season.

waypoints.name: Pickle Pass
waypoints.note: Gap below Spectre's serrated south ridge of hoodoos, visible from Frenzel Camp, where the technical climbing on the route begins.
waypoints.directions: From the col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, staying roped near the pocket glacier. Phantom's west and south ridge is the usual second bivy and where most parties stop for the night. Pickle Pass itself can hold snow well into the season, and the first-ascent party found it snowed over and skirted it rather than crossing.

waypoints.name: Spectre Peak
waypoints.directions: From the base of the south ridge, start up right of the entry notch: about 100 ft of fourth class leads into blocky 5.7 climbing, then low-fifth ground to a large tree-dotted ledge and a traverse left onto the crest proper. The crest gives sustained 5.4 to 5.8 climbing past the crux third pitch, a short overhanging band of 5.9 choss above sparse gear on the face right of a mossy gully, and past a shattered gendarme at pitch 7 where a 25 m rappel into the gap is followed by a self-belayed ascent of the far wall. The last pitch weaves through narrow, chalky hoodoo towers to a 30 m rappel off the final tower onto a big grassy ledge, from which about 600 ft of third and fourth class with a couple of low-fifth moves leads to the top.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: I-90 Exit 52, Alpental ski area parking lot; approach up valley past Source Lake toward Pineapple Pass basin for NE Face/Catscratch Couloir.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52 and head north on Alpental Road to the Alpental Ski Area, where the trailhead starts from the parking lot at about 3,100 feet.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large gravel lot at the end of Alpental Road (1.5 mi past I-90 Exit 52); Northwest Forest Pass required to park.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52 and follow Alpental Road to its end, about 1.5 miles, where a large gravel lot at roughly 3,100 ft serves as the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

waypoints.name: Source Lake junction
waypoints.note: Signed spur splits toward the Source Lake overlook; leave the Snow Lake Trail here and head off-trail toward Great Scott Bowl for the South Face approach.
waypoints.directions: From the lot follow the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north, climbing steadily through forest for about two miles and 1,000 ft to the small signed fork where the Source Lake spur splits off. Bear toward Source Lake. This is the last of the maintained tread — everything above it is off-trail.

waypoints.name: Great Scott Bowl talus/snow field
waypoints.note: Off-trail talus (snow-covered into early summer) beneath The Tooth's south side; loose rock and overhead rockfall risk from parties above, helmet recommended once you leave the trail.
waypoints.directions: Watch on the left as the trail curves for the point where a continuous talus field starts running alongside it, and leave the tread there. Traverse west into the boulders, losing a little height at first, then climb back up toward The Tooth's obvious south-facing wall by whatever line through talus and lingering snow gives least resistance. Helmets go on here: the bowl is loose and parties above will knock rock down it.

waypoints.name: Notch south of Pineapple Pass
waypoints.note: Gain this notch on the ridge just south of the true pass, then contour clockwise (exposed sidewalk traverse) to reach Pineapple Pass proper.
waypoints.directions: Work up the bowl aiming for the gully just left (south) of the prominent pointed rock partway up, and take that to the second notch south of the south face rather than trying to gain the pass directly. Early in the season this is a sustained steep snow climb that warrants an axe and sometimes crampons. A moat where the snow has pulled back from the rock often guards the last step onto the crest.

waypoints.name: Pineapple Pass
waypoints.note: Named saddle where pitch 1 of the South Face begins; a moat where seasonal snow pulls away from the rock can make the final step onto the col tricky into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: From the notch drop a short way down the far side, contour clockwise around beneath The Tooth, and climb back up to the pass. It is Class 3 to 4 but short and not exposed. The col is where the first pitch starts, so this is the place to rope up and sort the rack.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed rock traverse near the top of pitch 4 — the real crux of the climb despite the 5.4 rating; stay roped and protect it well.
waypoints.directions: Four short pitches of low fifth-class lead up from the pass: a groove trending right on juggy rock, connecting ledges past a pair of trees, an easy fourth-class ramble, then the steeper headwall. The Catwalk is the left-hand finish of that last pitch — a narrow, balancy ledge with a great deal of air beneath it. Two easier finishes exist to the right, and a steeper crack further left for parties wanting harder climbing.

waypoints.name: The Tooth summit
waypoints.note: Small, exposed summit block with views of Chair Peak, Bryant Peak and the Alpental valley; begin the four-rappel descent back to Pineapple Pass from anchors here.
waypoints.directions: From the end of the Catwalk a few metres of unroped scrambling tops out on the small summit block. There is no continuation off the far side — everyone comes back down the face they climbed — so keep the party gathered and organised for the rappels rather than spread across the top.

waypoints.name: Smithbrook Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small dirt lot (~15 cars) off FR 6700; Northwest Forest Pass required, no potable water or restrooms.
waypoints.directions: Drive US 2 to the Smithbrook Road turnoff, Forest Road 6700, about 4.2 miles east of the Stevens Pass summit — roughly half a mile east of milepost 69 if you are coming from the Leavenworth and Wenatchee side, or about 68 miles out from Everett and Seattle. Follow FR 6700 about 2.7 to 3 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead at around 4,000 feet, on the left. The gravel road is normally passable to passenger cars once it is snow-free, but it is not plowed in winter; then you park at a pullout on the highway shoulder and add miles of road travel each way. The trailhead is a small dirt lot for about 15 cars, with no potable water and no restrooms.

waypoints.name: Rainy Creek tributary crossing
waypoints.note: Only reliable stream on this route — top off here, nothing higher on the ridge.

waypoints.name: Union Gap - PCT junction
waypoints.note: Smithbrook Trail #1590 switchbacks up old growth to this saddle and ends at the PCT; leave the maintained trail here for the boot path.

waypoints.name: Boulder field below the SE ridge
waypoints.note: First left off the PCT at a ~10-ft dead snag; boulder field lies to the north — follow cairns lined up with the snag to the field's high point.

waypoints.name: SE ridge avalanche slope
waypoints.note: Steep, brush-choked slope gains the southeast ridge; brush is very slick when wet or snow-covered and this line is avalanche-prone on all aspects — not recommended in unstable snow.

waypoints.name: Union Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit, no maintained trail; open views down the Rainy Creek valley and along the PCT corridor toward Grizzly Peak.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Corrected - previous waypoints incorrectly placed this route ~59 miles away at Amphitheater Mountain (Pasayten Wilderness), a research error. South Peak is actually part of the Gunsight Range, Glacier Peak Wilderness - same remote 2-day approach as Middle Peak (Downey/Bachelor Creek trail to Itswoot Ridge, Dome-Chickamin col, Chickamin Glacier).

waypoints.name: South Peak (Gunsight Range)
waypoints.note: A real, distinct summit — the southernmost of four named summits (Northeast/North/Middle/South) along one short ridge crest, reached last in a north-to-south traverse after Middle Peak. This coordinate is a disclosed geometric estimate ~0.2mi south of Middle Peak's position (48.30571,-120.99439) along the ridge, not a directly measured fix.

waypoints.name: Wine Spires / Silver Star Trailhead (SR-20 MP 166)
waypoints.note: Pullout ~4mi east of Washington Pass, signed for Silver Star Mountain, serving the whole Wine Spires cluster including Paisano Pinnacle.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the pullout near milepost 166, roughly 4 miles east of Washington Pass at about 4,300 feet. This is the Wine Spires parking and it serves the whole cluster, Paisano Pinnacle included. Park on the shoulder — the boot path drops straight off the pullout down talus toward Early Winters Creek, so no further driving is needed.

waypoints.name: Bench Camp spring
waypoints.note: Fresh water at the Larch/Bench Camp below the Wine Spires cirque; reached via steep climbers trail from the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166.

waypoints.name: Paisano Pinnacle - Summit
waypoints.note: Classic 7-8 pitch West Ridge to the summit.
